News.title: Minister to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

News.title: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles
News.content:
The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.

King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

News.title: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who is one of the corporation's best-known news anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vain thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, Moshiri was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

In a few cases, PV can develop into another type of blood cancer called myelofibrosis, and even more rarely can develop into a type of leukaemia called acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), according to charity Blood Cancer UK which funds research into blood cancers.

News.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
News.content:
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.

The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.

It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

On Sunday night in Portsmouth protesters were involved in a stand-off with police near the Eastney Landing ferry port, where small boat occupants had been brought to shore.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy.

A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."

They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

News.title: Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, says football's world governing body.

Infantino, who has filled the role since 2016, has been under pressure following his scrapped plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment firms.

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

"The Fifa president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," read a Fifa statement.

"Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election."

Infantino refused to answer questions about his future when asked by reporters at the Women's Under-20 World Cup in Poland on Saturday.

It is the first time Fifa has said he will run for a new term since the plan was announced following the summer's World Cup.

Should the 56-year-old Swiss be re-elected, he will serve until 2031.

Fifa this week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Last week Uefa filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
News.content:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

News.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
News.content:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

News.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
News.content:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Raise the Colours founder charged with 14 offences
News.content:
The founder of an activist group which has been putting Union Jack and St George's Cross flags on lampposts has been charged with a string of offences including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault.

Ryan Bridge, 45, of Blackwell, Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, has been erecting flags in the Midlands and the south of England since last summer as part of Raise the Colours.

Thames Valley Police said Bridge had been charged with 14 offences from a two-month period in Oxfordshire earlier this year.

He is due to appear at Oxford Magistrates' Court on 3 November.

The offences are:

Seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress

Three counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence

Two counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress

One count of racially aggravated fear of violence

One count of common assault

In July, Oxfordshire County Council was granted a High Court injunction to stop people placing flags near highways because of safety concerns, trespass and obstruction.

Birmingham City Council has applied for a similar injunction which will be heard at the High Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Three charged with attempted murder after shooting
News.content:
Two adults and a teenager have been charged with attempted murder after a shotgun was fired in a town centre.

Police were called to Market Place in Braintree, Essex, at about 22:10 BST on Monday following what officers described as a "targeted attack".

Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, and a 17-year-old from Braintree who cannot be named for legal reasons are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations including:

Attempted grievous bodily harm with intent

Possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence

Possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence

Possession of a firearm while prohibited for life

Harassment

Malicious communications

Possession of a shotgun with intent to cause fear of violence

News.title: Two killed as car hits group of cyclists
News.content:
Three people have been arrested after a car crashed into a group of cyclists, killing two riders.

Kent Police said a white Ford Focus was travelling along Sole Street in Cobham near Gravesend just before 07:50 BST on Sunday when it was involved in a collision with three cyclists.

Two of the cyclists - a man in his 60s and woman in her 50s - were confirmed dead by emergency services on the scene, the force added.

Their next of kin have been informed.

A third cyclist was taken to a local hospital for treatment with minor injuries, according to officers.

Two men aged 20 and 21 were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Kent Police said the road was closed while an investigation took place.

The force is now appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident or saw the car or cyclists before the crash to contact them.

News.title: Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms
News.content:
Scots should not have to travel further for health care under the government's plans to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two, John Swinney has suggested.

The BBC asked the first minister about the impact of such changes for people who are already travelling long distances - such as women living in the far north who have to travel 100 miles down the A9 to give birth in Inverness.

Swinney said it would "not be my intention" for people to travel further, with initial modelling showing the country divided into two east and west health boards.

He also said he could not put a "specific figure" on NHS job losses, but he had been "open about the fact that public sector employment will fall".

News.title: Body-worn cameras given to school crossing wardens
News.content:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to Â£1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.

Incorporating laughter therapy into treatment plans could help ease respiratory difficulties in patients suffering from a widespread lung condition, new research indicates.

Scientists behind the study suggest that the "simple, low-cost" intervention performs on par with conventional breathing drills and may work to "complement existing care" for individuals living with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

In the UK alone, an estimated 1.7 million people suffer from COPD, including roughly 600,000 who remain undiagnosed.

The clinical trial evaluated 63 patients diagnosed with COPD who were receiving care at Ankara Bilkent City Hospital in Turkey.

Researchers assigned a third of the group to laughter therapy sessions, while the remaining participants were guided through pursed-lip breathing routines or received no specialised exercises.

open image in gallery Rather than relying on an inhaler, people could turn to laughter therapy ( PA )

After being shown how to perform the techniques, patients were asked to complete 30-minute sessions three times weekly over an eight-week duration.

Respiratory function was evaluated before, during, and after the intervention.

Results demonstrated that both laughter therapy and pursed-lip breathing achieved measurable improvements compared to the group receiving no intervention.

Dr Goncagul Aldan, a lecturer and nurse at Hacettepe University Faculty of Nursing in Ankara, said: "People with COPD often feel breathless, even during simple daily activities. This reduces their quality of life and makes them increasingly dependent on others for care.

"Managing COPD requires more than medication alone. Patients need a holistic, approach to help them cope with their symptoms, the physical burden of the disease, and its emotional and psychological impact.

"With this research, we wanted to explore whether additional simple, low-cost techniques could complement existing care.

"Laughter therapy had already shown promising results in a number of other chronic conditions. Its accessible, enjoyable nature suggests it could equally benefit COPD patients, not only in coping with the daily stress of living with a chronic illness, but also in directly supporting their respiratory health."

Symptoms of COPD NHS The main symptoms of COPD are: shortness of breath, particularly when you're active

a persistent chesty cough with phlegm – some people may dismiss this as just a "smoker's cough"

frequent chest infections

persistent wheezing

The positive impacts of both interventions persisted a month after the programme concluded, Dr Aldan noted.

She said: "These findings offer hope that simple, low-cost techniques which patients can practice at home – without any equipment or specialist support – may reduce breathlessness and improve daily wellbeing.

"Both interventions also showed promising results in improving overall health, suggesting that laughter therapy may be a worthwhile area for further investigation alongside pursed-lip breathing in COPD care.

"In COPD, the airways tend to collapse during exhalation, trapping stale air inside the lungs.

"Pursed-lip breathing creates a gentle back pressure that allows this trapped air to escape, slows the breathing rate, and helps patients feel more in control of their breathing.

open image in gallery Laughter therapy could help millions in the UK ( PA )

"Laughter may exercise the breathing muscles, promote deeper exhalation, and trigger the release of endorphins, offering both physical and emotional relief."

Further studies remain necessary to understand why laughter influences COPD symptoms.

Dr Aldan added: "Laughter therapy aims to evoke the effects of genuine laughter in the body. However, the mechanisms behind laughter therapy in COPD remain poorly understood, and more comprehensive research is needed."

The trial's findings will be presented at the European Respiratory Society (ERS) Congress in Barcelona.

Emma Rubach, head of health advice at Asthma + Lung UK, said: "This exciting study shows that laughter therapy is an effective way to control breathlessness for people with COPD.

"This research adds to growing evidence showing that innovative non-traditional therapies can improve people’s ability to manage lung conditions like COPD.

"While further studies with a larger number of patients are still needed, laughter therapy appears to be a fun, accessible and effective self-management technique to help people with COPD control their symptoms.

"While there is still no cure for COPD, which often leaves people fighting for breath, innovations like laughter therapy have real potential to provide genuine relief and improve the quality of life for the 1.7 million people in the UK who have the condition."

Luke Littler marked his return to the European Tour with a title after winning the Czech Darts Open, beating his great rival Luke Humphries in the final.

Littler has been managing his schedule this year and has not played a Euro event since the Belgian Darts Open in March.

But winning trophies is an insatiable habit for the 19-year-old and he ended Humphries’ reign in Prague with a 8-6 victory in the final, having earlier beaten Michael van Gerwen in the semi-final.

Humphries had not lost in this tournament since 2023 but Littler is his nemesis and now has a strong grip on their enduring rivalry.

The world champion claimed a sixth European Tour title, in just his 16th event, and he takes home a £35,000 prize.

“It’s what the fans deserved, obviously the two best going at it in a final once again. I’m glad I’ve won,” Littler said.

“I’m glad I can put my name over there (on the honours board). It’s good to be back.

“The rust has definitely gone, I am just happy to be back on stage, back in front of fans, back playing.”

With his place in October’s European Championship finals guaranteed – the final major title Littler has yet to win – he is not expecting to play in any of the three remaining regular Euro tour events.

“Not sure now I’ve won this one. I think I think I’ve secured my place in Dortmund,” he said. “Dortmund’s obviously the one I’m chasing.

“And then in two weeks’ time, it’s the World Series in Amsterdam. Yeah, we’ll have to see what happens, see what the plan is, see how busy I am.”

Despite sweltering temperatures inside the arena in Prague, Littler kept his cool throughout, starting off his day with a last-16 win over Krzysztof Ratajski.

He then whitewashed Danny Noppert 6-0 in the quarter-final before ousting Van Gerwen 7-3 in the last four.

Humphries is always a tough task, though, and, chasing a third successive title in Prague, the world number two led 4-3.

But Littler rattled off four successive legs to take control and then got the job done.

At least five people have been killed and five more injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, according to authorities.

The plane hit multiple vehicles and burst into flames, sending thick, dark clouds of smoke into the air Sunday afternoon.

The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft overran the runway and crashed while landing at around 2 p.m. The flight had been heading to Florida from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

“Five people lost their lives and five others were injured,” Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a press conference later Sunday. “My heart is with all of the families who were affected and to everyone who is grieving tonight, and we’re also praying for the injured and for their families.”

open image in gallery At least five people have been killed and five more injured after an Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport, according to authorities ( Reuters )

Photos and videos shared online appeared to show the Prime Air plane had come to a rest beside a roadway. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the airport to extinguish the blaze, officials said.

Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel confirmed the incident in a statement shared with The Independent.

“This is a fast-moving situation and we're still gathering details. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Nantel said. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was sending investigators and issued a full ground stop at Miami International as emergency crews responded to the crash.

open image in gallery The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft, which was heading to Florida from Puerto Rico, crashed while landing at around 2 p.m. ( Reuters )

During a ground stop, all flights are put on hold and the airport is essentially shut down.

The ground stop has since been changed to a ground delay by the FAA.

Travelers can expect average delays of more than six hours until Monday at around 4 a.m.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it was “gathering information” about the crash.

Tyson Fury has suggested his all-British blockbuster bout with Anthony Joshua is off and has challenged Oleksandr Usyk to a third fight.

Fury and Joshua have been locked in negotiations over a mega-money bout but the ‘Gypsy King’ has grown impatient at a lack of confirmation, calling his rival a “coward” earlier in the week.

Fury has now said Joshua has “s**t his pants” and turned his attention to Usyk, who he lost twice to on points in 2024.

“AJ has s**t his pants again, yet again,” he told his followers in a post on social media. “After 11 years he has finally s**t his pants yet again.

open image in gallery Anthony Joshua wanted the fight to take place at Wembley (John Walton/PA) ( PA Wire )

“This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk. Oleksandr you’re his (Joshua’s) trainer and his sensei and you know he is a weak minded piece of s**t and that he would never fight the Gypsy King, which you have had the guts to do twice.

“You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. Good luck to you, let’s do it again. Let’s run it back in November. The ball is now in your court… do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling quits? Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent.”

Joshua’s promotor, Matchroom’s Eddie Hearn, has previously said an agreement hinged on his client’s net purse.

New York’s Madison Square Garden was widely expected to be announced as the venue despite Joshua’s camp preferring Wembley Stadium as Sela, the Saudi state-owned promotional company financing the fight, wanted a bigger American audience on Netflix.

Iliman Ndiaye has explained why he turned down Tottenham to join Manchester City by saying his determination to play Champions League football counted against Spurs.

The Senegalese winger completed a £60m move from Everton to City on deadline day but only after Tottenham were the first to bid for him.

Spurs were discussing a £60m move for Ndiaye – with Richarlison returning to Everton for £35m in a separate deal – but as soon as City showed an interest, the former Sheffield United player decided not to join a club that finished 17th in each of the last two seasons.

“For me it was always going to be City,” he said. “I wanted Champions League and playing at one of the best teams in the world. I'm not saying Tottenham is not, but when Manchester City comes through, you don’t say no.

“This is where I think I belong. I've worked hard to get to this point. When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League.”

Ndiaye spoke to City manager Enzo Maresca before making the move, adding: “He’s someone that admired me and as soon as they came through I had only one direction where I wanted to go.”

Ndiaye made his City debut in Saturday’s 1-0 win over Coventry, and while he came off in the closing stages, he allayed fears he was injured by saying it was cramp.

Donald Trump’s energy chief hesitated to say whether gas prices would go up or down, with the midterms only two months away.

Then, he cautiously said he thought they would go down, after saying that he “didn’t want to have an opinion” on whether the national average fuel price would continue to hover around $4 a gallon for the fall.

“Look, I don't want to have an opinion on that, but if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today, it’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday.

Wright spoke to CNN’s Dana Bash on State of the Union and claimed that the end of the summer travel season would decrease demand enough to lower gas prices around the country, or at least in states where elected officials are following the administration’s lead and loosening gasoline blending requirements.

Right now, AAA reports that the average price of gas is $4.147 per gallon in the United States. Gas prices have been more than a dollar higher on average since the beginning of the year, when the president launched a war with Iran that has become increasingly unpopular with even his own voters.

Trump has repeatedly insisted that Americans are buying gas for well below that amount as he seeks to prevent a Republican electoral bloodbath in the midterm elections.

open image in gallery Energy Secretary Chris Wright declined to say when he thought gas prices would begin to drop on Sunday ( CNN - State of the Union )

In the same interview, Wright could not say that the actual cause of higher gas prices — the Iranian seizure and attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz — was no longer an issue.

Asked by CNN whether merchant ships traversing the strait were safe, Wright contended that any who coordinated with the U.S. Navy would be able to safely cross the waterway. The Navy has been escorting a limited number of vessels through the strait for weeks, using a channel close to the Omani coastline.

“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week, signalling that negotiations between Washington and Tehran were not taking place. “I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement.”

“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” the president added. “They are just playing out the inevitable.”

The restrictions on free transit continue to reduce the number of tankers able to cross the strait every day, meaning that pressures on the global energy market remain in place as long as only partial use of the waterway is feasible. Some companies are still refusing to coordinate with the U.S. Navy, and even more view the risks as untenable even with U.S. support, citing deadly drone and mine attacks on vessels. Several have been struck by mines or drones even while traveling the Omani passage with U.S. escorts.

open image in gallery Vessels awaiting transit through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become the focal point of the Iran war ( Reuters )

Bash, noting that August was the deadliest month for commercial shipping crews operating in the Strait of Hormuz since shortly after the conflict began, asked Wright if he could guarantee that merchant vessels would soon be able to travel the strait safely.

“We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit,” Wright claimed, while admitting the strait’s traffic was not at “pre-conflict levels.” More than a dozen civilians have died on attacks against merchant vessels and ports since the conflict began in February.

He was then pressed by Bash to answer the question, and said: “Well, if they want to work with the U.S. Navy, I think they can. Look, we're trying to end a 47 year conflict, as Iran dashes to develop nuclear weapons, and wreak havoc on their neighbors, and threaten the world economy.”

Vice President JD Vance said at a press briefing this past week that the administration hadn’t seen any evidence to suggest that Iran was reconstituting its nuclear program after strikes the U.S. launched in late February and early March. Experts have questioned whether Iran even attempted to do so after U.S. strikes hit those same sites last year.

Dozens of demonstrators have descended on Portsmouth after migrants headed towards the Hampshire coast on a small boat were intercepted and brought ashore.

Video footage showed protesters facing up to police and shouting “stop the boats” on Sunday evening. Far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, an associate of Tommy Robinson, was live-streaming from a beach in Eastney and encouraged his supporters: “To get in your cars and get down here now”.

Emergency services rushed to intercept the small boat on Sunday evening, with two RNLI lifeboats called out and a HM coastguard helicopter and plane also deployed.

Around 140 migrants are believed to have disembarked near Eastney in Portsmouth, and will be taken to Manston immigration centre in Kent for processing.

A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: “In response to a report on 6 September of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams.

“Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire Police and South Central Ambulance Service were also sent.”

Reform leader Nigel Farage claimed that the boat had launched from Baie de Seine, near Caen, saying: “Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. This is a joke”.

The French maritime prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said on Sunday that around 140 migrants had set out on a small boat from the west of the Baie de Seine overnight on Saturday. The departure was “unusual for the area”, with small boats usually launched from further up the French coast near Dunkirk.

The French maritime prefecture said on Sunday that the “migrant boat is currently continuing its journey towards the United Kingdom”, after people on board refused assistance.

open image in gallery Police officers at the scene near Eastney Beach, Portsmouth, where protesters have gathered, after a small boat thought to be containing asylum seekers and heading towards the coast sparked a major response with a helicopter, aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. ( PA )

Footage taken from the scene near Eastney showed a large emergency presence, and men wrapped in blankets were seen being taken ashore on RNLI boats.

Christine Martin, who was on a boat on the Eastney Cruising Association pontoon, told Portsmouth’s The News that she was unable to leave due to the incident. She said: “Being on my own in the boat, I am a little bit worried. The coastguard has been here sometime not letting anyone in or out. I just don’t know what to do.

“There have been lots of ambulances turning up. There is may 50 or 60 police and ambulance officers down near the Hayling Ferry pontoon.”

Conservative MP for MP for Isle of Wight East, Joe Robertson, posted on social media on Sunday: “Extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west.

“We don’t know if this migrant boat was headed for the Isle of Wight but I’ll be contacting the Home Office first thing. We need to know exactly what happened and if new routes are being used for mega-dinghies by people smugglers.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.

“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.

“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40 per cent more boots on the ground on French beaches.”

In a new post, President Donald Trump used an apparently AI-generated image to falsely portray Robert De Niro — long one of his sharpest critics — as a supporter.

The image, one of dozens shared by the Republican president on Truth Social on Sunday, shows the 83-year-old A-list actor holding up a red shirt that reads: “TRUMP IS MY PRESIDENT.”

Trump captioned the post: “Even this jerk is beginning to get it,” suggesting De Niro has had a change of heart.

De Niro, whose film credits include Taxi Driver, Goodfellas and Raging Bull, has established himself as one of the president’s most outspoken and persistent detractors in Hollywood.

In 2016, ahead of the presidential election, the Manhattan-born actor called Trump a “pig,” a “punk” and a “bulls*** artist.” Three years later, he described the president as “evil,” adding: “I can’t wait to see him in jail.”

open image in gallery The image, posted by the Republican president on Truth Social on Sunday, shows Robert De Niro holding up a red shirt that reads: “TRUMP IS MY PRESIDENT” ( @RealDonaldTrump, Truth Social )

“I don't even use the word ‘hope’ anymore with [Trump's] administration. They have to be gotten out,” De Niro told USA Today last month. “He's just going to destroy not only the country, but other parts of the world. It's insane. That's a big concern of mine, and I think a lot of people now.”

Trump has lobbed his own share of harsh words at De Niro over the years.

“I never knew how small, both mentally and physically, Wacko Former Actor Robert De Niro was,” the president wrote on Truth Social in 2024. In a separate post that year, he wrote: “Robert DeNiro has a terminal case of Trump Derangement Syndrome. Such a stupid sounding guy, a low IQ individual!”

open image in gallery Trump has a long history of public feuds with Hollywood actors, including Alec Baldwin, Brad Pitt and Meryl Streep ( Getty Images )

The 80-year-old president has also feuded publicly with a string of other Hollywood stars across his two terms, including Rosie O’Donnell, Alec Baldwin, Brad Pitt and Meryl Streep.

He has also previously used AI-generated content to mock celebrities who have criticized him.

News.title: Maitland-Niles’ last-gasp debut goal salvages Everton’s miserable week
News.content:
At the final whistle, the first song the stadium DJ played was Spirit of the Blues and how those relieved Evertonians lapped it up after a week of angst.

Their team had been on the precipice of a defeat that would have exacerbated all the frustrations that bubbled away following the chaotic conclusion to the transfer window. Indeed, it was 10 seconds over the allotted five minutes of added time when the ball fell to Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

It had been three years since the former Arsenal full-back had played in the Premier League – his last goal in England was on October 30, 2019, in an EFL Cup tie with Liverpool at Anfield that ended 5-5 – and he would not have joined Everton if their attempt to sign Kenny Tete from Fulham had not failed.

But here he was 30 yards from goal, with no need to break his stride as Manchester United’s backtracking defenders presented him with an invitation to shoot. So that’s what he did. With one perfectly timed swish of his right foot, an unlikely hero transformed the mood of a club.

News.title: Arsenal teach Chelsea a lesson in how to be champions
News.content:
This is how champions are supposed to play and, although the Arsenal home support have not seen a team defend their place at the apex of English league football for two decades, they knew it when they saw it.

The chase was on for Mikel Arteta’s team within two minutes when Morgan Rogers, the man who might have moved to Arsenal this summer, put his new club Chelsea in the lead. So unfolded a thrilling 100 minutes of Premier League competition. Arsenal were the better team in terms of ambition and attack even if one could not discount Chelsea until the very last moment.

Others might have crumbled. That Chelsea did not will give Xabi Alonso hope for a team that did not feature the injured Moisés Caicedo and is now without the departed Enzo Fernández. Yet he will also recognise that his childhood friend from San Sebastián in the other dugout has created a side that treated the game, and their place in it, with an urgency that looks different. The first two minutes might have been ragged for Arsenal but after that they did not let the game happen to them.

News.title: Kimi Antonelli’s stunning home Italian GP victory all but seals first F1 title
News.content:
The 20-year-old also benefited from a perfectly-timed (from his perspective at least) mid-race virtual safety car when Lance Stroll retired his Aston Martin, which allowed Antonelli a cheap stop to switch to fresh mediums while Russell stayed out on used hards. But at some point you just have to take your hat off to the youngster.

Antonelli was irresistible. He had already surged from 19th on the grid to 12th by the time the red flag came out at the end of lap 2. He was up to sixth a couple of laps after the race resumed. And by lap 18 of a 53-lap race, he had passed Russell for the lead for the first time. That is some going.

Having caught up to Russell, the two Mercedes drivers engaged in an entertaining battle for a few laps, the pair of them yo-yoing in and out of the lead before Russell got past Antonelli on lap 23 and managed to make it stick.

But the key moment of the race came on lap 27 when Stroll stopped at the first chicane and the VSC came out. For Antonelli, the decision to switch to fresh mediums was clear. He was going to struggle to make it to the end of the race. Far better to drop a few positions and fight back on fresh rubber.

For Russell, it was far trickier. He was in the lead of the race. He was on hard tyres which he knew could get to the end of the race. And he also had the problem of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who at the time he was struggling to shake off.

Mercedes chose to keep Russell out there. In hindsight, it may have been the wrong decision. Had he stopped at that point, he would at least have stayed ahead of Antonelli, and on the same tyres. By staying out, he kept the lead but found himself relentlessly hunted down by the Italian.

By lap 49, the Italian had caught up to him. Antonelli botched his first attempt at reclaiming the lead, going wide onto the gravel at the first chicane. But he made no mistake one lap later as Russell was once again left licking his wounds.

News.title: VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling
News.content:
“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

News.title: Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fight back for draw
News.content:
A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

News.title: Relentless Springboks give All Blacks 15 minutes of hell to lead series
News.content:
There will be no repeat of the All Blacks historic Test series victory in South Africa 30 years ago, after the home side ruthlessly ensured they will lead 2-1 going into the concluding weekend.

And the manner in which the Springboks blew away their fierce rivals in the last 15 minutes made Rassie Eramus’s men overwhelming favourites to finish the job in America next Saturday.

However, there were passages of this brutal battle that suggested that Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry could still produce a finale worthy of the billing if New Zealand can learn the lessons from this brutal encounter at the FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

There was a late Kiwi try to give the scoreboard a humdinger hue but Erasmus’s side were well deserving of their second victory in as many Saturdays over their fierce rivals, and credit to the South Africa coach for outwitting counterpart Dave Rennie without needing to change his starting XV just before the kick-off, like he did seven days before.

Amazing what one can do with a simple but chilling game plan. The old scoundrel knew that if he slowed it down and let his scrum walk round the All Blacks scrum that his backs would have the precious space.

Yet, however it might feel away from Springbok turf, New Zealand will still fancy their chances of levelling it, especially after matching their opponents’ haul of four tries. Their fly-half, Ruben Love, missed five simple-enough points and until that last quarter it was an even contest. Yet, as it tends to, South Africa’s physical intensity and their almighty scrum eventually prevailed.

News.title: Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

News.title: ‘It’s just a useless gimmick’: Telegraph readers react to Dyson’s latest gadget
News.content:
Would you spend over £400 on a toothbrush? Telegraph readers aren’t convinced.

The new Dyson CameraJet has just launched, retailing for £419.99, which brushes, flosses and mouth-washes in one, with the help of a camera.

After Rebecca Astill gave her verdict on the gadget, we asked Telegraph readers for their views and whether Dyson can convince them to trade in their old faithfuls.

They share the toothbrushes they swear by, from manual to electric models, and whether they see any reason to upgrade. Here’s what they had to say.

Why readers are unconvinced

The majority of readers seem unconvinced by the CameraJet, with John arguing that a toothbrush and a smartphone “sounds like two accidents waiting to happen. Squirted in the eye with mouthwash as you drop the phone down the toilet”.

“It’s just a useless gimmick,” argues reader Donald Mckie, a retired NHS dentist. “The average patient wouldn’t have a clue what they would be looking at in their mouth on a phone screen,” he adds.

“Dyson as a brand is an aspiration for many but I don’t know how this appliance would improve anyone’s oral health.”

In his view, “the tank for the mouthwash at 12.5ml is far too small, the industry average will be somewhere near 250-300ml” to last long enough and successfully dislodge sticky plaque.

He also questions the picture quality of the camera with water spray, saliva, lips, facial hair and toothpaste in the way. “People nowadays will expect pin sharp detail, which I doubt this will deliver.”

Sports.title: 'Just unheard of! - Antonelli's miracle win likened to 'walking on water'
Sports.content:
On a Monza weekend that had already produced one implausible result in qualifying, Italy's new young star Kimi Antonelli delivered a second in Sunday's thrilling race to ensure its own prominent place in Formula 1's history books.

Of course, unlike surprise pole position sitter Pierre Gasly - who had never previously qualified at the head of an F1 grid in 190 appearances spent in mostly midfield cars - the 20-year-old Antonelli has become a fixture at the head of the field this year.

Sunday represented the seventh race win of the Mercedes driver's increasingly-impressive second of Formula 1 and one which extended what stood as a 59-point championship lead to a joint season-high 66 points.

But by winning from the second-lowest grid position in F1's 76-year history - 19th place - and beating a team-mate and chief title rival in George Russell who had started from the front row, Antonelli ensured it was anything but just another win.

And that's before you even consider the local factor too - Antonelli ended a 60-year wait for an Italian to win their home Grand Prix again.

The remarkable Monza comeback led to Antonelli being described as "King Kimi" by Martin Brundle, who has both raced against and commentated on many of the sport's most legendary figures over more than four decades.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Italian Grand Prix.

Brundle's fellow Sky Sports F1 pundit Nico Rosberg, the 2016 world champion, was similarly effusive in his praise after witnessing Antonelli's remarkable drive.

"We have to say the race that he drove, the first lap, the second start, everything was to perfection," said Rosberg.

"The speed he had, how he was managing everything. You cannot do it better.

"He's in his second season in F1, he just turned 20. Who does that like that? It's just unheard of!"

'He's going to walk over water' - Wolff thought 'special moment' was possible

Rosberg had been among the many ahead of the race to suggest that a podium was likely out of Antonelli's reach from the grid's penultimate row, something the Italian himself had ruled out after qualifying.

But it turns out that not everyone was expecting it to necessarily be a race purely of damage limitation from the grid penalties that had left Antonelli so out of position.

"I thought one of the two [Mercedes drivers] is going to win," disclosed Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff after the race.

"Either George because he was on pole [for the restart] or Kimi because he's going to walk over water here in Monza. And I felt that yesterday also."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli and George Russell go wheel-to-wheel for the Italian Grand Prix lead in several epic team-mate battles.

Wolff, who worked with Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes for six of the Briton's seven world titles, said he sensed "a special moment" was potentially in the offing from Antonelli at his home track.

"Its been a while that I've seen drivers' energy levels, mindset or behavioural pattern and I knew that that was his mission today, to win the race," he said.

"I chatted with his father yesterday, the father also saw that coming.

"These are the moments where you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions, that a special moment could come.

"It's still a mechanical sport, so it can change quickly."

What made the difference for Antonelli?

Like any great comeback story, Antonelli's was not without some good fortune along the way.

Certainly, the second race start after the red flag for Charles Leclerc's big lap-two crash offered a second chance to make up multiple places more quickly than otherwise might have made the chance had the race not been stopped, even if it did compromise Mercedes' plans for running Antonelli on a long hard-tyre opening stint.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc CRASHES OUT the of the Italian GP

He was already running 12th by the time the red flag was thrown. He then picked up four more places on the restart lap. By lap 13 he was directly behind Russell in third and, once Gasly's early challenge faded, the Mercedes' went head-to-head from lap 16 in what soon turned into an almost lap-by-lap changing of the lead.

Eventually running second as the battle settled down slightly, a later well-timed Virtual Safety Car then allowed Antonelli to make a pit stop to switch on to fresher medium tyres, with Russell soon locked in to going to the end on more-worn hards, although Wolff said it was not clear at the time which strategy would win the race.

In any case, Wolff believes it was Antonelli's driving on track overtaking cars that made the difference.

"The differentiator today was the ability going through the traffic," added Wolff. "We've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis put it in some of the races and that's what he's shown today.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli wins the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid

"There's just no stopping when a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them."

As for Italy's rising star himself, Antonelli said he had woke up on Sunday morning feeling "very good mentally" and "that a very good result would have been a podium for me".

"But after the red flag I was already P12 and I had another start," he added.

"After another couple of laps I was already in the top five and I knew I could have a shot for the win. Of course it was very difficult to break away but we managed to pull it off and bring it home."

Sports.title: Great Britain and Ireland claim historic win in Walker Cup thriller
Sports.content:
Great Britain and Ireland won the Walker Cup for the first time since 2015 after a nerve-shredding late comeback saw them beat the USA by a 13½-12½ scoreline.

Dean Robertson's side looked to be heading for defeat after suffering a clean sweep of defeats in the Sunday morning foursomes and with the Americans three points ahead going into the singles matches.

But the home side lost only two of the 10 matches and the competition eventually came down to the very last as Josh Hill won the 18th hole of his match with Tyler Watts to seal an incredible victory.

The USA will be left to regret the late turnaround after four missed putts to retain the Walker Cup.

Team GB&I needed a quick start to produce any sort of comeback and they delivered after Stuart Grehan, Luke Poulter - son of former Ryder Cup star Ian - Jack Whaley and Tyler Weaver all won their matches.

However, the Americans steadied the ship after securing halves through Miles Russell and Kihei Akina and wins courtesy of Ryder Cowan and Josiah Gilbert as it looked like they had thwarted the comeback.

As it looked like the Americans were about to take a firm grip on yet another win, Team GB&I responded once again. Eliot Baker overcame Stewart Hagestad on the final hole to ensure the Walker Cup would be determined on the final hole.

Hill and Tyler Watts were all square coming down the last at County Clare and Hill produced a stunning up-and-down from the bunker to complete a thrilling comeback and seal the unlikeliest of wins.

Speaking after securing the decisive point, Hill said: "This is absolutely unbelievable. It doesn't get better than this."

Captain Robertson added: "I believed in the team the whole time. They worked so hard. They played so well."

This is just the tenth time GB&I have won the Walker Cup.

Sunday foursomes: Clean sweep for USA

The morning session saw GB&I lose all the momentum they'd claimed on Sunday as the USA comprehensively won all four matches to move into a three-point lead.

Home captain Robertson stuck with his pairings from Saturday, but his players struggled to perform and failed to take the lead in any of the four matches.

The demise started as Grehan and Baker were beaten 3&2 in the opening match of the day by Stout and Fang.

Leng Jr. and Akina took out Poulter and Easterbrook by 4&3 in the second match, while Russell and Watts had little trouble in overcoming Weaver and Graham 3&2.

In the final match, the USA duo of Jennings and Cowan took the lead against Sheils Donegan and Hill on the second hole and never looked back, taking a 4&3 victory to leave the visitors needing just 3½ points in the afternoon session.

Sports.title: 'There are no rules here' - Hamilton criticises Ferrari after Leclerc clash
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has accused Ferrari of having "no rules" after a clash with his team-mate Charles Leclerc during the Italian Grand Prix.

Hamilton launched an aggressive move up the inside of his team-mate at the first corner, but was then forced off onto the gravel himself on the exit of the chicane as Leclerc held onto the inside line.

Hamilton dropped from his starting position of fourth to 10th, and was left playing catch-up for the rest of the race, as he eventually finished sixth.

Leclerc held onto third after the incident, which featured contact between the pair, but then crashed out of the race on the second lap, leaving Ferrari to suffer a dismal afternoon at their home race.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Italian Grand Prix.

"I think it comes down to rules of engagement," said Hamilton, who joined Ferrari from Mercedes in 2025.

"When I was at Mercedes, we had written rules of engagement.

"We never really, really had it too bad. There was a moment between me and Nico [Rosberg] a couple of times, but more often not, it was good.

"Here, there are no rules. We need to address that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc crashes out of the Italian GP

Too late or too early for team orders?

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli claimed a stunning victory from 19th at the grid to extend his advantage over Hamilton to 76 points, while the Ferrari driver also fell 10 points behind George Russell as the Brit completed a Mercedes one-two.

It had been a topic of discussion in the media before the race as to whether Ferrari should prioritise Hamilton over Leclerc given his advantage in the standings, which was extended to 36 points by Sunday's result.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton says the team are 'too late' to implement any sort of 'Ferrari priority'.

Asked by Sky Sports F1 after the race whether he should have priority over Leclerc, Hamilton replied: "We are too far past that already. It's too late for that now.

"I lost a lot of points today to those guys.

"We will do our best to keep pushing the rest of the season but they are out now, out ahead of us."

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur insisted that it was too early in the season for the team to prioritise one of their drivers.

Vasseur justified his position by using the example of McLaren's experience last year, when Oscar Piastri led Lando Norris in the standings before being hauled in by both his team-mate and Max Verstappen by the end of the season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Karun Chandhok was at the SkyPad to look at who was at fault after Lewis Hamilton went down to 10th position after this contact with Charles Leclerc.

"For sure, the outcome of the first corners is not good for the team," Vasseur said.

"Now, to see if we have a team order or whatever, I think that the good comparison that I made was that last year, Piastri was leading McLaren at this stage of the season and if McLaren put everything on Piastri, Max Verstappen would have been champion.

"For sure, at one stage you have to take a decision but I think it was too early to take a decision before Monza. Now we have time to discuss with the guys."

Leclerc: We went too far

Leclerc admitted that he and Hamilton had gone "too far" in their early battle, but questioned who was "forcing" a narrative playing the team-mates off against each other.

The Monegasque referred to the previous race in Zandvoort when Hamilton had been left frustrated by being held up by Leclerc during the race when the pair were on different strategies.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc explains what caused the Ferrari driver to crash out in the early stages of the Italian Grand Prix.

"I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other," Leclerc said.

"I mean, honestly, Zandvoort, there was way too many talks already.

"Here, it's true though that we went too far. I think Lewis in Turn 1, then Turn 2, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough - and doing it here is not good."

Should Ferrari have pitted Hamilton?

Hamilton was also once more left frustrated by his team's strategic decisions, with the 41-year-old questioning both the choice of tyre compound for him after the early red flag, and a later decision not to pit him under a virtual safety car.

"It's one of the harder ones to swallow today," he told Sky Sports F1. "I was definitely hoping for more.

"I gave it absolutely everything. We just didn't have the speed on the straights and we were mostly a sitting duck to the guys around me.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nico Rosberg says it is 'not feasible' for Ferrari to favour Lewis Hamilton at this stage of the season.

"We will look internally and try and figure out what we could have done better. I felt we should have been on the hard tyre [on the restart] but we also would have had to overtake people, because we were further back than we were supposed to be.

"I thought they were going to stop us [under the VSC] but they didn't stop us, so I ran out of tyres."

Vasseur said that Ferrari's difficultly overtaking due to a lack of straight-line speed meant they would have struggled to make an extra stop work in the way that Antonelli and Verstappen, who finished third, were able to.

"We were 10 seconds behind Max before the VSC and we finished 10 seconds behind," Vasseur told Sky Sports F1.

"If you do this [pit], you have to overtake and overtaking is not our favourite topic. It would have been more difficult."
