World.title: U.S. and Iran trade attacks on ships as fighting flares up again
World.content:
U.S. and Iran trade attacks on ships as fighting flares up again

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

The U.S. military on Saturday said it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Navy ships were targeted by missiles, with the retaliatory attacks part of a flare-up in fighting this week following a month-long lull.

U.S. Central Command said it struck the vessels after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched two ballistic missiles at two Navy warships patrolling the sea. CENTCOM said a U.S. aircraft carrier and missile destroyer "successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" and that no American personnel were injured.

"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours," CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on social media. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Sponsor Message

Strikes between the U.S. and Iran resumed last weekend, after a month's break from the fighting, when the U.S. hit several sites in Iran in response to a threat of Iran firing sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

An Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf, a key hub for the country's oil-export system, was one of the three vessels the U.S. struck on Saturday. A tanker in the Gulf of Oman also was hit in "multiple critical locations" and its crew had to abandon ship and another tanker near Jask was also struck, CENTCOM said.

The three Iranian oil tankers were part of a "multibillion-dollar shadow network" that funds the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and its regional proxies, CENTCOM also said in the statement.

Shadow fleets are vessels that operate outside of the official shipping system. Iran uses shadow fleets as a way to move oil because it is under sanction. The U.S. has seized Iranian vessels operating under shadow networks, including two in April.

Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth on Saturday said in a social media post that if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, "we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."

Sponsor Message

"All they have to do is not shoot at @USNavy," Hegseth wrote.

Iran's foreign ministry on Saturday condemned the U.S. strikes, saying that they are "a clear violation of Paragraph 4 of Article 2 of the United Nations Charter, constitute a war crime, and represent an overt threat to international peace and the security of commercial shipping," according to the country's state media.

Lt. Col. Ebrahim Zolfaghari also warned Iranian forces would target American military in the region "more severely than before" if the U.S. continues strikes against ships, according to Iran's state media.

Iran said Sunday it had targeted an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the U.S. military. Iran did not mention casualties.

NPR's Carrie Khan in Tel Aviv and Jane Arraf in Beirut contributed to this report.

World.title: Amazon cargo plane strikes multiple vehicles after overrunning Miami runway
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, striking multiple vehicles and bursting into flames in a crash that sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and forced the closure of all runways at one of the busiest airports in the U.S.

More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the crash, arriving to find the aircraft on fire as crews worked to extinguish the flames and assess patients. Officials had not yet released information on injuries or deaths.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the aircraft overran the runway at about 2 p.m. local time after heading into Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue officials said the plane struck multiple vehicles after leaving the runway.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was sending investigators and issued a full ground stop at Miami International as emergency crews responded.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway with two semi-trucks parked nearby, according to images on social media. Images showed the plane on its belly and largely intact despite the fire.

All runways and taxiways were closed, an airport spokesperson said. The FAA warned that delays were likely to persist even after the airport reopened, with arrivals and departures expected to resume at a reduced rate.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it was "gathering information" about the crash.

Amazon said in an email to CBC News that it was also gathering details.

"We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," a spokesperson wrote.

"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved. We're doing everything we can to support those affected."

World.title: Elbows up or down? Why Alberta is diplomacy-first in the trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta’s top U.S. diplomat says playing nice is paying off for his province in the Canada-U.S. trade war.

Nathan Cooper, Alberta’s senior representative to the United States, told CBC’s West of Centre that compared to provinces that have taken a more aggressive approach, Alberta has come out ahead.

“I think the premier’s diplomacy-first approach has really not only been helpful for me, but certainly helpful for the province,” Cooper said.

“If we look at the impact of U.S. tariffs on the Alberta economy, we have a disproportionately low impact.”

Experts have said while Alberta’s industries are not immune to the impact of the trade dispute, they are not seeing the direct hit other provinces are. Despite the trade war, the U.S. continues to increase its imports of Canadian oil.

The comments come as Cooper, the former speaker of the Alberta legislature, spent time in Nashville, Tenn., with Premier Danielle Smith last week.

Cooper said American officials have been “significantly more responsive” to his team than some of his provincial counterparts.

Alberta is the only remaining province with no ban or retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol imports. The province’s position on that is something the Americans have shown “a real appreciation” for, Cooper said.

“I believe that that's actually translated into results for the province of Alberta,” he said.

The premier said her trip to Music City was a personal one, but she took time to meet with business and tourism leaders while there. Ahead of her trip, Smith also appeared on U.S. news networks pushing for a return to the bargaining table.

Honey or vinegar?

Not everyone has been on board with Alberta’s approach.

Following Smith’s trip to Mar-a-Lago last year , she was called out for not being a part of a unified “Team Canada” response.

This summer, Premier Doug Ford pushed for Canadian leaders to take a stronger stance, and called for energy exports to be cut off to the U.S.

Smith’s predecessor, Jason Kenney, has said a modest tax on oil exports should be considered to put extra pressure on the president.

Smith has rejected both ideas and consistently said doubling down on diplomacy is a better approach.

“I think in this scenario, maybe Premier Smith is seen as a dissenting voice or not quite on script,” Evan Menzies, vice-president of Crestview Strategy said in an interview.

Premier Danielle Smith met with business and tourism leaders while on vacation in Nashville, Tenn., last week. (Danielle Smith/X)

But Menzies, who previously worked as a director of communications for Smith’s party, said things look more favourable for Alberta when you zoom out.

“If you're to look at what's bearing good fruit, Alberta's efforts seem to be bearing some good fruit.”

Smith’s too-friendly-to-resist approach contrasts against Ontario Doug Ford’s aggressive advertising and insult slinging .

Cole Hogan, a strategic communications advisor at Alberta Counsel who has worked on Ford and Kenney campaigns, said the divergent tactics make sense considering domestic priorities.

“Ford's approach, while it makes a lot of people feel good … it hasn't garnered the same results that Smith's approach has here in Alberta.”

“They both have different political goals in doing so — they have different industries to serve.”

Separation anxiety

All this comes amid a looming election in Alberta on whether to hold a binding referendum on separation — something U.S. officials are increasingly waking up to.

It's been used by representative Andy Harris to trumpet renewed calls for a 51st state and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as a sign of disunity and failed trade talks.

On the ground, Cooper said the referendum isn’t frequently raised in his meetings with U.S. officials.

“At the end of the day, one of my key jobs is to try to determine the difference between signal and noise and do what I can to get people focused on the big issues that are impacting our province.”

World.title: 'We really weren't prepared for that': Torrential rain batters Cape Breton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A torrential downpour dumped more than 200 millimetres of rain on parts of Cape Breton over the weekend, destroying roads, culverts and bridges while triggering local states of emergency across three counties.

Nova Scotia RCMP say a 46-year-old Cape Breton woman reported missing Saturday morning was found dead later in the day in a flooded area of Richmond County.

First responders recovered the woman's body around 2:30 p.m. AT on Saturday near Kempt Road in Cleveland, N.S. Search crews initiated the response after her vehicle was discovered parked near her residence on the far side of a flooded bridge.

RCMP stated the death is not considered suspicious, though police did not elaborate. When asked whether the death was related to the flooding, police had no comment.

Richmond County Warden Lois Landry said she has never seen rain like this, comparing the destruction to hurricane damage.

"I think what struck me was [seeing] trees down on properties and across roads," she said. "And we really weren't prepared for that."

WATCH | Cape Breton battered by torrential rainfall as local states of emergency in effect: State of emergency declared in 3 Cape Breton counties after storm, flooding | Duration 4:12 Three counties in Cape Breton have declared local states of emergency due to severe flooding and widespread damage. Some areas got more than 200 millimetres of rain this weekend. The alerts from each county were jointly released on Saturday. The storm washed out roads and caused power outages across the region.

She said residents were expecting a typical rain event like those the island sees multiple times a year, but instead faced an unprecedented weather event.

She is not the only one who thinks so.

"We've never experienced anything to this size and effect," said Terry Doyle, CAO for Port Hawkesbury, N.S. "And certainly, that's what I'm being told by others as well."

Doyle spoke Sunday from an emergency response co-ordination centre where representatives from Victoria, Inverness and Richmond counties and the province are gathered. A state of emergency was declared Saturday for those three counties.

An RCMP vehicle drives through water from a brook that overflowed on Route 4 near South Side River Bourgeois, Richmond County. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Doyle said the bulk of the damage is in Richmond County, around Bras d'Or Lake, where floodwaters have washed out numerous roads, bridges and driveways.

Emergency Management Minister Kim Masland said it's difficult to give residents a timeline for repairs, as officials are assessing damage and more rain is expected to fall.

Dawn Chisholm, a resident of Richmond County, watched from her window as water crept up from a nearby creek closer to her home than she had ever seen. She walked down her washed-out driveway and saw that roads were flooded a metre or more deep.

"It was shocking when I got down to the end," Chisholm said.

Now, her home is sandwiched between two roadblocks. She said neighbours have helped each other with necessary supplies like food, but so far there has been no communication on when the road will be drivable.

She is new to the community, but said she went through something similar when her apartment building flooded in Halifax during a rainstorm about three years ago.

Chisholm said this "far outweighed what we went through" in Halifax.

She believes the state of emergency could have alerted residents earlier.

Angel Frost shared that concern. While her family in False Bay, N.S., was fine during the storm, she worried about her sister and two children in Arichat. They lost power for 11 hours and remained cut off by closed roads.

"The state of emergency, I feel like it almost has been called too late," Frost said Sunday while the order was still in effect.

Municipal leaders are urging residents to stay home so emergency crews can safely repair infrastructure.

Inverness County Warden Bonny MacIsaac echoed that plea, warning drivers that covered roads may be structurally unstable beneath the water. Anyone who must travel should check provincial road conditions at 511 first, she added.

Widespread washouts have left some residents stranded. Amanda Mombourquette, councillor for Richmond County District 4, expressed concern for vulnerable residents cut off from emergency services and essential groceries.

Part of the West Bay Road washed out at St. Georges Channel, about 25 kilometres west of St. Peter's, N.S. (Tom Ayers/CBC)

Nova Scotia Power's outage map showed more than 1,000 customers provincewide without power as of Sunday morning, primarily in Chéticamp, down from 5,000 earlier in the day. The outage number dropped below 200 Sunday evening.

Coun. Claude Poirier, who represents Chéticamp on Inverness County council, said the local Legion and fire department have opened comfort centres so residents can charge devices or get hot drinks.

Cape Breton municipalities have established a toll-free support line at 902-625-7888 for residents to report non-emergency storm issues.

In a statement posted to social media Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government is ready to provide any needed support and is in contact with provincial officials.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: B.C. drought forces volunteers to rescue salmon from drying streams
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Parts of British Columbia have been hit hard by drought this summer.

In Bessette Creek, severe drought conditions recently prompted orders limiting water use in an effort to protect salmon populations from record-low flows.

Temporary protection orders for the Salmon River watershed were also issued at the end of July, rescinded in early August to address increased wildfire risk in the region and then reissued at the end of August.

And those are just the watersheds struggling to the point of government intervention.

Bob Crandall is treasurer of the Cowichan Lake Salmonid Enhancement Society on Vancouver Island.

The society cares for 16 streams connected to Lake Cowichan, and Crandall says they are getting drier each year.

To help, the society does what they call fry salvage — manually rescuing fish from drying rivers and moving them into other waterways.

Ben Lorenson, left, and Aivars Liepa Spence releasing rescued fry from Robertson River into Lake Cowichan. (Submitted by Bob Crandall)

"I believe if the hand of man has caused these difficulties in the ecosystems, then the hand of man should be out there, trying to make an improvement to the problems," said Crandall, who has been doing this for over 16 years.

While B.C. communities are embracing this intervention as one of the few options available to them, scientists warn this has limits and may not be a good long-term solution.

Efforts to move fish

Together with the Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation and a variety of volunteers, Crandall works to gather fish — mainly salmon, trout and char — and carry them somewhere with more water.

But the work is becoming more difficult as the climate changes. The society has been doing fry salvage since 1984, and Crandall is used to seeing a kilometre or two of rivers and streams dry up over the course of a summer.

But that is no longer the case.

"We have noticed that streams are drying up farther upstream," he said.

"Now, it seems as though we're going five, six and seven kilometers upstream — it's just a lot more effort."

Bob Crandall, left, and Ben Lorenson containing fish to move them into pails for transport to Lake Cowichan. (Submitted by Bob Crandall)

The process involves aerators and bubblers to ensure the fish have enough oxygen, as well as nets to transport them. Crandall says carrying 23 kilograms (50 pounds) of water, fish and equipment across cobbled, dry streambeds can be challenging in hot weather.

He was born in a rainbow trout hatchery, so he has been around fish his whole life, and it is important to him that they remain part of the ecosystem rather than simply dying.

"You can rescue up to 100,000 or 150,000 fish during the course of a drought summer," he said.

Importance of fish

The Ts'uubaa-asatx Nation is also a major part of the fry salvage efforts. Its members help relocate the fish and use drones to determine where streams are drying up.

Crandall called the Nation the best partner the Society has ever had and says much of the work would not happen without it

"It takes an army of people to do it," said Aaron Hamilton, the Nation's operations manager.

Hamilton said that it's been challenging lately because there is no longer a normal pattern to follow. The weather can be extremely hot one month, followed suddenly by heavy rain.

Coho salmon fry and cutthroat trout fry gathered at Meade Creek. (Submitted by Bob Crandall)

Michelle Corfield, the lands and resource director and negotiator for Ts'uubaa-asatx, said salmon are a keystone resource for the community. The recovery projects are important to the Nation, she said, and it has also invested its own money in the work.

"Salmon are in our DNA," she said. "And it's up to us to ensure that we have salmon for today and into the future."

Corfield says the Nation takes a full life-cycle approach to salmon conservation, including river restoration and conditions in the oceans, rather than focusing only on individual fish.

Challenges to fry salvage

Similar rescue efforts are facing limits elsewhere as drought and extreme heat intensify.

This year's drought has been especially severe in France, and Jean-Pierre Faure of the Fédération de Pêche du Rhône said relocating fish is no longer working for them.

Faure says that there have been multiple weather events that would normally be expected only once every 50 to 100 years.

"The last one this summer is the worst we have ever had," he said. He added that France's management programs are not prepared for the changing conditions because they rely on the past to plan for the future — an approach he says will no longer work.

"It began very early in the end of May and since that time we have had four or five very big heat waves, reaching temperatures we have never seen before."

La Vauxonne, a small French river, in July 2026. (Fédération de Pêche du Rhône)

River flows were so low that fish were forced to gather in very small volumes of water, intensifying competition for food and shelter and causing more deaths.

Faure said fish experience physiological stress and lose energy when water temperatures rise above 18 or 19 C. He said juvenile fish are first to be affected because they have fewer energy reserves, while temperatures above 25 C can be fatal within hours.

"This summer, due to the combined effects of climate change and warm water discharge from the nuclear power plant industry, the average temperature of the Rhône River reached 25 degrees for more than two months," said Faure.

"It's still the case, it's still going on. This has never been seen before."

He said that instead of focusing on short-term interventions such as rescue fishing, the priority should be ecosystem restoration and water-use management.

Moving fish can add stress and cause injuries or spread disease, he said. The work can also cost at least 1,000 to 2,000 euros a day for each kilometre covered.

"When you have thousands of kilometres of rivers that are drying, it's not realistic to go and do this at a large scale."

He also said that when 90 per cent of the watershed is dry, there may simply be nowhere to move the fish.

World.title: Far-right AfD party takes big lead in regional German election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Germany's far-right AfD party has taken a commanding lead in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, with exit polls putting it at around 44 per cent of the vote. It remains unclear whether the party will secure enough seats to form Germany's first far-right state government since the Second World War.

The far-right Alternative for Germany was projected to win a strong victory in a regional election Sunday, but it wasn't immediately clear whether it would be able to fulfill its ambition of forming the country's first far-right state government since the Second World War.

The party of Germany's unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, was set for a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany's candidate for governor said that "we have written history."

Ulrich Siegmund, 35, told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that "things cannot carry on like this" and that it was "also a signal toward Berlin." Of Germany's unpopular leader, he said: "A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz."

Alternative for Germany, or AfD, went into the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern on its own. That would overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties' refusal to work with the AfD.

A first state government would be the biggest prize in the party's 13-year history, at a time of widespread discontent with an unpopular national government that has yet to persuade voters it can get the country's sluggish economy moving.

Whether or not AfD can form a government, the projected result is a blow to Merz, whose centre-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years. Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn't yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.

AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany's national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located.

WATCH | How the AfD rose to prominence in Saxony-Anhalt: How Germany’s AfD escaped the far-right fringe in Saxony-Anhalt | Duration 7:09 For the first time since the Nazi era, a far-right German political party is eyeing victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. For The National, CBC’s Marina von Stackelberg goes there to find out how Alternative for Germany (AfD) went from fringe to frontrunner.

Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is one of several classified as a proven right-wing extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, which points to members' denigration of migrants from Muslim countries among other things.

The party talks of "remigration," a politically charged term for the deportation of immigrants. Its leader in a neighbouring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.

AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism and says they're politically motivated.

Mainstream parties lose ground

Projections for ARD and ZDF public television, based on exit polls and partial counting, put AfD at a bit over 44 per cent of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.

That was far ahead of Merz's Christian Democratic Union which was seen polling 18 per cent and losing about half its support. The Left Party, the centre-left Social Democrats and Greens were seen taking around 9 per cent each.

It was unclear whether the BSW party would get the 5 per cent of the vote needed to win seats. The projections put AfD at least marginally short of an absolute majority, though that could change.

Officials prepare absentee ballots for the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sunday. (Liesa Johannssen/Reuters)

AfD's national co-leader, Alice Weidel, described the projected result as "sensational" and said that "we have received a very clear mandate to govern here." The party's "hand is outstretched to all who want to make Saxony-Anhalt better and move Germany forward," she said.

A visibly disappointed incumbent governor, Sven Schulze, congratulated AfD on becoming the state's strongest political force and said that "we as the CDU will also have to deal with this result," without specifying how.

Franziska Hoppermann, the national general-secretary of Merz's party, rejected the idea of backing off its refusal to deal with AfD.

"AfD is a right-wing extremist party. It wants to leave the euro; that would be economic downfall ... it works closely together with Russia, it wants a completely different social model," she said. "We will not work with them."

There already has been one case in which AfD won a state election but didn't end up governing. That was two years ago in neighbouring Thuringia, where a CDU governor took power with a minority government, but against a regional AfD that was well short of a majority.

If the result allows Schulze to try to put together some kind of alliance with smaller parties, that would be delicate, because it would require at least some tacit support from the Left Party, a hard-left party with which the CDU refuses to form coalitions.

States' powers

Germany's 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system.

Siegmund has listed among his top priorities "a deportation offensive" and dropping incentives for people to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about "disinformation."

AfD in Saxony-Anhalt wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag and ensure they fly the national flag. It opposes taxpayers' money being "given away" to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.

State governments also sit in Germany's upper house of parliament, which has to approve some government legislation. The influence there of Saxony-Anhalt, one of the smaller states in a nation of 83.5 million people, is limited — it controls four of the 69 votes.

World.title: Trailblazing Indigenous actor and director Georgina Lightning dead at 63
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Indigenous filmmaker and actor Georgina Lightning has died at the age of 63.

Her daughter, Crystle Lightning, announced the news online late Saturday night, just before 11 p.m., though no details about the cause of death were shared.

Social media posts link her death to the Enoch Indian Relay World Championship at the Enoch Park Race Track, an event Lightning posted about on her Facebook page just one day before her death was made public.

Enoch Cree Nation announced in a statement on Saturday that it “is mourning the loss of a community member following an incident that occurred during [Saturday’s] Indian relay event.” The nation did not confirm the identity of the person who died.

RCMP told CBC News Sunday that officers were called to the Enoch Park Race Track shortly after 6:30 p.m., where a woman had died before police arrived.

Police said the woman who was killed was standing in the media area, but would also not confirm her identity.

RCMP said that Occupational Health and Safety will take over the investigation.

Born in Edmonton, Lightning was a member of the Samson Cree Nation, located about 100 kilometres south of the city.

In addition to her impact in the film industry, she was widely known as an outspoken advocate for First Nations causes.

More to come.

World.title: Counter-tariffs won't just affect the cost of goods for Canadians. They'll hit the trailers moving them too
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians bracing for billions of dollars in counter-tariffs won't just see prices rise on American aluminum, toilet paper, furniture and more — but on the very semi-trailers hauling those goods into and around the country.

Ocean Trailer, the largest retailer of semi-trailers in Western Canada, is waiting on a $45-million order of 600 trailers from U.S. manufacturers.

The company is rushing to get as many over the border before a 25 per cent Canadian counter-tariff on trailers, and scores of other items, takes effect on Tuesday.

"The extra cost, the 25 per cent, is well above our profit margin on a trailer, so we would have no choice but to pass that along to the customer," said Mack Keay, Ocean Trailer's chief operating officer, told CBC News from Vancouver.

The federal government announced dollar-for-dollar countermeasures will take effect at 12:01 a.m. on Tuesday on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods , in response to the latest round of tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump's administration.

Keay said it's possible Ocean Trailer may be able to cancel some of its order, which was expected to flow in trailer by trailer until the end of the year, but it's on the hook for the trailers that are already in the process of being fabricated in the U.S.

The ones the company can't get into Canada by Sept. 8 will have to be parked somewhere in the U.S. or sold to American-based retailers, and Keay said he wouldn't get back what he paid for them.

Industry 'very much concerned'

Ocean Trailer isn't alone.

The head of the Manitoba Trucking Association said the vast majority of semi-trailers in Canada come from the U.S.

"I know a number of members that currently have trailers on order and are very much concerned about the cost of those trailers, because they ordered them before the counter-tariffs," said executive director Aaron Dolyniuk.

"I don't know that they'll be able to afford to pay 25 per cent more for them when they get here."

Dolyniuk said many businesses that rely on those trucking companies to ship product are also "rushing to get things north of the border before the [counter-]tariffs come on."

"I was talking to one member late last week … [who] said normally, they hauled two loads for this one customer northbound, and they wanted 15 this week," he said.

A variety of types of semi-trailers are towed along Canadian roadways, but the two most common are called dry vans and refrigerated vans.

The latter, also known as "reefer" vans, haul groceries, pharmaceuticals and other items that need temperature-controlled conditions during transport to avoid spoilage.

Dry van trailers are used to haul everything from kitchen appliances to car and machine parts, paper products, furniture, televisions, canned goods and other non-perishable items.

'This is not going to be OK'

There are just two semi-trailer manufacturers in Canada — one based in Ontario that doesn't manufacture reefer van trailers and another in Quebec which does, along with making dry vans, flat fright vans and other specialty trailer types.

Neither would have the capacity overnight to absorb the increased demand for trailer orders or rentals from Canadian trucking companies following counter-tariffs.

Ocean Trailer's Keay said Canada's domestic manufacturing capabilities are less than half of what the trucking industry would need to meet demand.

At the industry level, the potential added costs from counter-tariffs are eye-watering.

The average cost across trailer varieties is about $75,000, said Keay. A 25 per cent tariff would drive that closer to $95,000.

Each of the seven Ocean Trailer branches from Manitoba to B.C. is bringing in one or two trailers per day, either associated with orders from trucking companies or to be added to the company's rental fleet, said Dallas Senebald, the branch manager for the Winnipeg office.

"This is not going to be OK. Not just us not being OK, the industry is not going to be OK," said Senebald, whose Winnipeg office employs 40 people.

"There will be a shortage of trailers, which then increases demand, increases the cost of the trailers, and that gets filtered down right to consumer goods that are needed to be shipped."

If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt. - Aaron Dolyniuk, Manitoba Trucking Association

Senebald said trends in semi-trailer sales can be unpredictable year to year, depending on supply and demand of goods that need shipping.

One year, a larger corporate customer might order 100 trailers for purchase, and then none the next year, said Senebald. The Winnipeg branch might bringing in 300 to 400 trailers one year, and 80 the next, he said.

The variability is one reason the industry relies on a mixed model. Ocean Trailer has about eight suppliers — seven in the U.S. and one in Mexico, said Senebald.

On top of being the largest retailer of semi-trailers west of Ontario, it's also the largest business for rentals.

In the short term, Canadian trucking companies may turn to rentals as they hold off on buying U.S. trailers that cost them 25 per cent more due to counter-tariffs, said Senebald — and that's a concern.

"Demand for rentals is going to skyrocket so much so that we probably won't have enough to fulfil customer needs," he said.

"Saying no to customers repeatedly is never a good thing. Eventually, they stop calling."

The trucking association's Dolyniuk said the depth of pain felt will ultimately depend on how long the tariff war goes on.

"If this lasts many weeks ... there could be companies going bankrupt within the trucking sector and outside of it," he said.

World.title: How Prince Harry and Meghan's return to Britain is setting off 'shockwaves'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hello, royal watchers and those intrigued by what's going on inside the House of Windsor. This is your deep dive into royal news and analysis. Reading this online? Sign up here to get this delivered to your inbox.

After Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as working members of the Royal Family and settled in California in 2020, there was little to suggest they would want to return to the United Kingdom any time soon.

So it came as a considerable surprise when word broke that Harry, Meghan and their two children were on their way back and would settle outside London for an extended period.

"It seems so counterintuitive and so contradictory to everything that they have said since the moment they left," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

But now they're back, and even though there has been much telegraphing of the idea that Harry and Meghan are not going to be working royals again, the move carries broader implications for both the institution of the monarchy and other members of the Royal Family.

"Regardless of whatever their reasons are, their return creates massive shockwaves," Vovk said.

WATCH | Prince Harry and Meghan returning to U.K.: Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K. | Duration 2:06 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace has confirmed. The couple will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens.

"What does this mean for Harry and Meghan as a couple? What does this mean for Harry and Meghan and their children as a family unit? How will this impact relations with the rest of the Royals?

"How will the monarchy respond to this? How will the British public respond to this? How will in particular the tabloid and the predatory media respond to this? How will Harry engage with the media in light of his wins and losses in court over the past year regarding media intrusions?"

Harry and Meghan have their supporters and detractors, and as much as they have stepped back from official royal duties, what they do and say continues to draw attention.

"They may not be working royals, but they're still members of the Royal Family," Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway, University of London, said in an interview.

"Harry is the son of the King at the end of the day, and he will never not be the son of the King."

For the monarchy, Harry and Meghan's return could divert attention from day-to-day activities of the House of Windsor.

WATCH | Reaction in London to Harry and Meghan's return: Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K. | Duration 2:25 The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly returning to Britain this month – six years after they quit royal duties and relocated to the U.S. While details around the decision behind their shift are unknown, the British public has mixed feelings about the move.

"Officially, nothing changes," Prescott said. "But clearly, Harry will get attention wherever he goes, whatever he does, and so there is a sort of risk of that being a distraction from the work of the monarchy."

To avert that, Prescott sees a need for "some element" of communication between Buckingham Palace and Harry and Meghan.

Vovk sees their return as potentially a new "crisis point" for the monarchy.

"It all depends on how things are handled on both sides. We know the palace is going to — and they've already taken the position — that [Harry and Meghan are] not working royals, 'we won't be commenting on their lives now that they're back.'

"So a lot will depend on how Harry and Meghan proceed."

How they proceeded over the past few years — in what became a visible estrangement from the wider Royal Family — included several instances of pointed criticism of the monarchy and the family itself, whether through their interview with Oprah Winfrey , a Netflix docuseries or publication of Harry's memoir Spare .

Prince Harry, right, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, walk along the boardwalk after meeting volunteer first responders from Bondi Surf Bathers Life Saving Club during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, on April 17. (Jonathan Brady/The Associated Press)

More recently, there has been no public criticism, and with King Charles, there appears to have been some rapprochement.

Harry, Meghan and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, visited with the King and Queen Camilla privately when they were in the U.K. last month, prior to word breaking of their return.

"You can imagine at the personal level [King Charles] would want to see his son and the children, as I assume Camilla would at one level," Prescott said.

"But … Harry did single Camilla out for criticism in [Spare] and … that dynamic would be interesting to know more about, how Camilla views all this."

There is, however, no sense that Harry's estrangement from his elder brother, Prince William, has thawed in any way. Much media speculation since the return has focused on how William and his wife, Catherine, Princess of Wales, will be feeling about it.

"We're probably not going to hear a word about anything from them because anything that is said, people will jump on, people will try to read into it," Vovk said.

Prince Harry, left, and Prince William, right, stand during the unveiling of a statue they commissioned of their mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, on what would have been her 60th birthday, in the Sunken Garden at Kensington Palace in London, on July 1, 2021. (Dominic Lipinski/The Associated Press)

For William, Prescott suggested, there could be a risk that there would come a point when — particularly if Charles is seen to be a bit more forgiving — that the lack of contact with his brother could start to look "quite surly and sulky."

"At some point, you may have to just let bygones be bygones and just move on and not hold a grudge for forever and a day."

The return also spawns numerous questions around issues that have been at the heart of some of Harry's most vocal grievances, whether over actions of the media — particularly the tabloids — or security for him and his family.

Still, it seems likely that whatever Harry and Meghan do will draw headlines, fuel much conversation on social media and continue to divide opinion.

"Anything that they do creates a public response because whether people like them or people hate them … there is clearly something about them that still activates public opinion," said Vovk.

He sees multiple reasons for that, one of the biggest being Harry is the younger son of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

People who have felt like they connected with Harry after his mother's death in 1997 have continued to feel that connection, said Vovk. He likens Harry to "a reflecting mirror that has a billion different reflecting facets on it, because there are so many millions and millions of people who take an interest in him."

"It says more about us … consuming celebrity culture than it does necessarily about Harry personally."

A new royal face on Canada's $20 bill

The portrait of King Charles is seen on the new Canadian $20 note at its unveiling in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Canadians just got their first glimpse of King Charles on the $20 bill. Our CBC friend Natalie Stechyson had this report:

It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian bank note to feature Charles , whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

In a news conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic." It's been more than 70 years since a new monarch appeared on a Canadian bank note. The late Queen Elizabeth first appeared on the bank's inaugural $20 note in 1935 as a young princess, Macklem added.

Two years later, in 1937, the bank's bilingual series featured King George on most of its bills. By 1954, with its landscape series , every note carried the portrait of Queen Elizabeth, until now.

The new bill is also historic because it "features security technologies never before used on a Canadian bank note," Macklem said.

"Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever."

Tiff Macklem, governor of the Bank of Canada, holds the new Canadian $20 note featuring the portrait of King Charles as he speaks during its unveiling in Ottawa on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation.

The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.

The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.

In a news release , the bank explained that the portrait of Charles is surrounded by a floral and leafy tapestry "inspired by the King's lifetime dedication to the environment."

Also on the front are provincial and territorial floral emblems representing the 13 provinces and territories. A circular window, which the bank explains is visible from both sides of the note, "features plants that are culturally significant to Indigenous Peoples in Canada."

As for security features, the note has a purple security stripe that includes elements that "spin, transform and pulse" when the note is moved, the bank said. This makes the bill "easy to check and hard to counterfeit."

WATCH | New $20 bill unveiled: Bank of Canada governor unveils new $20 bill | Duration 1:10 Governor of the Bank of Canada Tiff Macklem calls the new vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles 'visually stunning and more secure than ever.'

"The new $20 note reflects important parts of who we are as Canadians, honouring our Commonwealth roots and our ties with international allies," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in the news release.

"It honours our constitutional traditions through the portrait of His Majesty King Charles III and recognizes the service and sacrifice of Canadians through the Vimy Memorial, a symbol that continues to resonate across generations."

The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.

The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.

Back to royal work

Queen Camilla, centre, meets local schoolchildren during a visit to Spellow Hub Community Library in Liverpool, England, on Friday. (Peter Byrne/The Associated Press)

This time of year has a back-to-school, back-to-work, holidays-are-over feel to it, and that seemed to be the case for some senior royals this week, too.

After a traditional summer break at Balmoral in Scotland, King Charles and Queen Camilla had a noticeably busier roster of engagements over the past few days.

They were at the British Museum in London on Wednesday evening to view the historic Bayeux Tapestry .

Other engagements included Charles meeting the Pakistani national cricket team at Clarence House. Camilla was at the Royal Academy of Dance , and had engagements that focused on her literary interests in Liverpool on Friday.

On Thursday evening, Camilla also made a surprise appearance at an event that celebrates "the enduring power of literary correspondence," Buckingham Palace said.

Camilla read out loud a letter that was written by Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother after the death of her husband King George VI in 1952.

Queen Camilla, right, meets with members of staff and volunteers during her visit to the Ebony Horse Club to mark the youth charity and community riding centre's 30th anniversary on Thursday in London. (Henry Nicholls/Getty Images)

The notable uptick in royal engagements early in September is a change from the reign of Queen Elizabeth, who stayed much longer at Balmoral each summer.

"It's a slight modernization of … the royal calendar," said Prescott, who noted that there was a time when it was more based on the ecclesiastical calendar.

"The Queen just followed that rhythm of decades gone past, whereas [now] it's just more typical that September is a fully working month."

There is also, Prescott said, a sense that Charles likes his royal work, "so is perhaps, in a sense, itching to get back."

William to represent Charles at royal funeral in Norway

Charles, centre, then Prince of Wales, and Norwegian King Harald, second from left, arrive for a wreath-laying ceremony at the National Monument in Oslo on March 20, 2012. Harald died on Aug. 28. (Berit Roald/Scanpix Norway/AFP/Getty Images)

After the death last week of King Harald V of Norway , King Charles offered condolences and praised the late Scandinavian monarch for his " unwavering dedication," guiding his country "through times of great change with warmth and humility."

Charles also noted "close historical and family ties" between the U.K. and Norway, "with Britain one of the first countries to recognize Norwegian independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1905."

At Harald's funeral on Wednesday in Oslo, Charles will be represented by his son and heir, Prince William, Buckingham Palace announced Saturday. Princess Anne will also attend in a private capacity as godmother to the new Norwegian king, Haakon VII.

Who would represent the Royal Family in Oslo had been a matter of some curiosity.

"Everyone's asking me: 'Who will the Windsors send to the funeral?' because that is quite … significant," Vovk said.

"Over the last … 20 years, the Windsors have not done a great job in terms of participating in the royal community at things like funerals, investitures, those sorts of ceremonials."

King Harald, centre, arrives at Westminster Abbey in London on Sept. 19, 2022, for the state funeral service for Queen Elizabeth. (Marco Bertorello/AFP/Getty Images)

One possibility for attending Wednesday's funeral was Prince William. Prescott noted that tradition has held that the British heir to the throne attends such occasions.

Still, there has been some inconsistency around all of this.

"When Elizabeth the Second died, we … sort of just assumed that the kings and queens of everywhere else would come, and so there's a bit of unevenness there in that relationship," Prescott said.

Harald's funeral will be held in Oslo Cathedral. Other royals expected to attend include King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands , King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko of Japan.

Headlines have also focused on the Norwegian royal family since Harald's death, given the presence at a related event earlier this week of his disgraced step-grandson, Marius Borg Hoiby, and the expectation that he will be at the funeral .

Hoiby, who was convicted of rape in June, is the son of Harald's daughter-in-law, now Queen Mette-Marit, from a relationship prior to her marriage to now King Haakon. Hoiby is appealing his conviction and has received permission to attend the funeral.

Royally quotable

"The Bayeux Tapestry — or the Canterbury Embroidery, as it might just have been called — recounts a conflict. Yet here it is today, nearly a thousand years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

— King Charles, during a speech on Wednesday at a viewing of the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum. The fragile tapestry that depicts the 1066 Norman conquest of England is on loan from France for the 10-month exhibition.

King Charles, second from right, and Queen Camilla, centre, accompanied by French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, view the Bayeux Tapestry Exhibition at the British Museum on Wednesday in London. (Richard Pohle/Getty Images)

Royal reads

A senior equerry to King Charles and Queen Camilla who captured widespread attention online is to step down from his role supporting the Royal Family. [The Independent]

Sarah Ferguson will return to the U.K. after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports. [The Guardian]

Amid family feuds, damaging headlines and questions about its future role, the Royal Family has spent much of the past decade managing its public image. But the importance of good royal PR dates back centuries . [The Conversation]

Princess Ingrid Alexandra has stepped into a historic new role as heir to the Norwegian throne — and appeared to pay a touching tribute to her grandmother as she stood alongside her father at his swearing-in ceremony. [Daily Mail]
