World.title: Perfect Day Mexico wasn’t dead after all. Now its opponents are headed to the Supreme Court
World.content:
Perhaps someone should have driven a stake through its heart.

Royal Caribbean’s Perfect Day Mexico was widely believed dead in May, when Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena announced that the massive water park planned for Mahahual, Quintana Roo, would not be approved.

But the massive, US $1 billion extreme water park proposal wasn’t buried after all. Royal Caribbean withdrew its environmental application before authorities could formally reject it, leaving the cruise giant free to return with a revised proposal.

Now the residents’ battle has reached Mexico’s Supreme Court, which on Aug. 10 agreed to hear three challenges to fast-tracked land-use changes that helped make Perfect Day possible.

The stakes reach well beyond the fate of a water park. The fight involves development alongside the Mesoamerican Reef, the world’s second-largest barrier reef system; a national campaign that drew more than 5 million petition signatures; and now a potentially precedent-setting question: How much opportunity must Mexican citizens be given to challenge development decisions that could permanently alter the places where they live?

A reef transformed

When Luis Fernando Amezcua first began diving off Mahahual nearly three decades ago, he remembers a very different Caribbean: water about 5 to 6 degrees Fahrenheit cooler, with coral reefs alive with color and an extraordinary variety of marine life.

The reef is still remarkable. A first-time visitor could easily be dazzled by its diversity. But to Amezcua, the losses are impossible to miss.

If he could take a visitor anywhere in Mahahual, he said, he would dive with them directly in front of town. Then he would show them photographs of that same reef 20 years ago, and let the contrast speak for itself.

Mahahual’s problems don’t stop at the shoreline. Amezcua says the wastewater system is already overwhelmed in a town of roughly 3,000 residents, where a single cruise ship can arrive with 6,000 passengers — and as many as four ships may call in a day.

And on the Yucatán Peninsula’s porous limestone, what happens on land doesn’t necessarily stay there. Contaminated water can quickly move through the underground aquifer toward the sea, adding another source of stress to an already vulnerable reef.

For Amezcua, who has lived in Mahahual for about 17 years and belongs to the citizens’ collective Salvemos Mahahual, the issue isn’t whether the town should develop. It’s what kind of development — and how much the ecosystem can withstand.

From four stories to 20

Accommodating the company required changing the rules.

In December 2025, the municipality of Othón P. Blanco approved changes to the urban development plan covering 107.67 hectares — roughly 200 football fields — in less than three weeks, a process attorney Irma Morales says normally takes eight months to a year.

Among the changes: The maximum permitted height on part of the property jumped from roughly four stories to about 20 — just what Royal Caribbean needed for the record-breaking water park it was proposing. The company had touted Jaguar’s Peak, at more than 170 feet tall, as the tallest waterslide tower in North and South America.

Morales, an attorney with Defendiendo el Derecho a un Medio Ambiente Sano (DMAS), said the changes were approved without the studies and public participation required by law.

Residents challenged them in federal court.

Their cases never got as far as the environmental questions. They were dismissed because judges found that residents had filed them too late — in one case applying a 15-day deadline for citizens to respond.

But Morales said the residents hadn’t even known the land-use plan had been changed while that clock was running.

Environmental justice and the rights of communities

That dispute has now landed Mahahual before the Supreme Court. At stake is a broader question of environmental justice: How meaningful is the right to challenge decisions capable of transforming a community and its environment if residents have only weeks to discover those decisions, understand their implications and get into court?

The justices are not deciding whether Royal Caribbean can build Perfect Day. But their ruling could establish new ground rules for when and how communities across Mexico can challenge land-use decisions with potentially irreversible environmental consequences.

That could affect communities fighting tourism, real estate and industrial projects far beyond Mahahual.

How a local fight went national

Long before the federal government intervened, Mahahual’s fight had become a national cause. Local residents had been organizing for months when Greenpeace Mexico and other national organizations joined.

The response surprised even veteran campaigners. A Greenpeace petition opposing Perfect Day ultimately drew 846,646 signatures. High-profile Mexican content creators, including film critic Javier Ibarreche and travel creator Alan Estrada, spoke out against the project, while Mexican BTS and Taylor Swift fan networks mobilized their formidable social media reach behind the cause.

For Ornela Garelli, campaigns director for Greenpeace Mexico, Mahahual tapped into a wider backlash against tourism, real estate and industrial megaprojects that communities say threaten ecosystems while giving residents too little voice over what happens to their territory.

Perfect Day became a particularly potent symbol: an enormous artificial attraction proposed beside one of the planet’s great natural ones.

The project anticipated as many as 21,000 visitors a day — seven times Mahahual’s resident population — while a Greenpeace analysis warned of impacts to vegetation, groundwater and biodiversity.

The campaign appeared to work.

The victory that wasn’t

In May, Bárcena announced that Perfect Day would not be approved. Semarnat requested additional information from Royal Caribbean, later saying the company failed to show how significant environmental impacts would be avoided.

On May 19, before Semarnat issued a final ruling on the main Perfect Day application, Royal Caribbean withdrew it. Morales says developers sometimes withdraw applications facing likely rejection to avoid a formal denial, allowing them to return later with another proposal.

Amezcua and his fellow activists understood immediately what that meant.

Asked whether Salvemos Mahahual believed in May that the fight was finally over, his answer was emphatic: “Not for a moment.”

Royal Caribbean, meanwhile, has made clear it is not walking away from Mahahual. On a July 28 earnings call, CEO Jason Liberty told investors the company was continuing to work “to develop a tourism destination” there, saying negotiations with government and community stakeholders would “affect our previously planned timeline.”

That is precisely what worries Amezcua: that attention will fade before Perfect Day returns in another form.

After nearly three decades watching Mahahual’s reef change, his message is simple: “Everything we do has consequences for the ecosystem we inhabit.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: What would a move from CONCACAF to CONMEBOL mean for Mexican soccer?
World.content:
Following arguably Mexico’s best World Cup finish since 1986, rumors have circulated online about El Tri potentially moving from its throne in CONCACAF to the much tougher South American confederation known as CONMEBOL. With FIFA’s presidential election coming up on March 18, 2027, rumors have swirled around current FIFA president Gianni Infantino granting the Mexican Football Federation’s ambition to switch over to CONMEBOL and host Club World Cup tournaments in exchange for its vote.

Historically, Mexico has dominated in CONCACAF, with its biggest rival being the United States in World Cup qualifiers, Gold Cup matchups and even friendlies. The occasional scare from countries like Costa Rica, Honduras and most recently, Canada, has threatened Mexico’s throne at the top. But it never fell lower than the third-best team in the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football.

The reality of a move to CONMEBOL

That narrative changes if Mexico switches over to CONMEBOL, where it would have to win or tie enough games against nations like Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay to even think about qualifying for future World Cups.

It’s also worth noting that Liga MX teams would be eligible to play in the Copa Libertadores, which is the South American version of Europe’s Champions League, creating opportunities for Mexican pro teams to compete against the best of Latin America every season.

Even though it may be a daunting task for some fans, Mexico’s stellar performance in the 2026 World Cup gives lifelong fans like myself hope. El Tri won all of its group-stage games for the first time without conceding a single goal. Then, it won a knockout-phase game for the first time in 40 years. Then, it took eventual third-place finisher England down to the wire in a 3-2 loss at the historic Estadio Azteca in the round of 16.

A great mix of emerging talent like Julián Quiñones and young players like Gilberto Mora gives fans reason to be excited for the future if Mexico actually switches over to CONMEBOL.

New and greater challenges

There’s an old saying in sports: If you want to be the best, you need to beat the best. And if Mexico ever hopes to build off its momentum from the last World Cup, playing against quality footballing nations will benefit the squad.

Brazil has won the World Cup five times and has plenty of top players in Europe, including Vinicius Junior, Raphinha and Alisson Becker. Argentina has Lionel Messi and back-to-back World Cup finishes where it either won or finished runner-up. Colombia and Uruguay are also teams not to be taken lightly. But the good news is this will force players like Brian Gutierrez, Gilberto Mora, Mateo Chavez and Raul “Tala” Rangel to level up their games. All of them had their moments in the last World Cup, and that momentum needs to continue.

Being part of CONMEBOL also means playing in the Copa America, a tournament that will be Mexico’s next big test, whether it makes the switch or is simply invited to compete in 2028. A solid finish would strengthen Mexico’s position as an improving footballing nation capable of making deep runs among the elite.

Revival of old-school rivalries

Despite Brazil’s accolades on the global stage, Mexico has proven to be a worthy opponent over the years. In the 1999 Confederations Cup final, Mexico prevailed over Brazil 4-3 in front of 110,000 fans in Estadio Azteca. Mexico also upset Brazil in the 2012 Summer Olympics in London, beating a prime Brazilian squad 2-1 that included players like Neymar, Thiago Silva and Marcelo.

Mexico and Colombia also go way back, having played against each other in the 2001 Copa America final. The Mexican national team also has Colombian influence via Julián Quiñones, a Colombian-Mexican striker who was Mexico’s leading goalscorer in the last World Cup with four goals in five matches. It’s also worth noting Colombia was set to be the original host of the 1986 World Cup, but withdrew due to overwhelming stadium demands from FIFA — leading Mexico to step in its place, hosting what is now considered one of the greatest World Cups of all time.

The parallels between Mexico and many South American countries are endless, which can strengthen rivalries if El Tri ends up switching over to CONMEBOL. Looking at the drama leading up to Mexico’s 2-0 win over Ecuador in the round of 32, new rivalries may also be in the works.

Great economic opportunities

Though watching Mexico face off against the U.S. is always a treat, there isn’t much else for Mexican fans to look forward to between World Cups. It’s no secret that the Mexican Football Federation loves hosting friendlies with its American neighbors in cities like Los Angeles and Houston due to economic opportunities, but other nations within CONCACAF don’t present the same level of excitement.

Playing in CONMEBOL will change that and add more variety to El Tri’s calendar. Regular matches against Brazil, Argentina and Colombia will also attract South American fans — millions of people ready to pay top dollar to watch their respective national teams.

Not only can Mexico continue to play against the United States in friendlies, but it can also strategically host games in American cities with large Brazilian, Argentinian and other South American populations.

Would you rather see Mexico vs. a tiny island in a Gold Cup group-stage match or against Uruguay in a World Cup qualifier? Regular matchups against steep competition will not only make Mexican players better, but will also create buzz and excitement that won’t fade after a World Cup ends.

Do you think Mexico can thrive in CONMEBOL?

Like most rumors, the idea of Mexico switching over to CONMEBOL probably won’t materialize unless real action takes place. But if you want a taste of how well Mexico’s current national team could stack up against South American competition, three of its next four games are against Colombia, Peru and Chile.

So, do you think Mexico is good enough to compete against South America’s best? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: From the archive: To friend or not to friend other expats in Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a humorous look at the often thorny issue of friendships among expats.

Any foreigners who’ve been in Mexico for more than two minutes know this truth: expat relationships are complicated.

I read with interest Louisa Rogers’ article on expat relationships, and found myself nodding along to much of it. Feeling threatened by large numbers of new foreigners moving to my area? Check! Hyper awareness of my ratio of Mexican-to-foreign-born friends? Check! Complaining about “those other gringos” who are messing up some designated “elsewhere”? Oh my goodness, please don’t make me look in the mirror.

Friends unless proven otherwise

My policy these days is to keep a very light grip on everything from my friendships to my own ideological musings. I pre-like everyone now, purposefully rather than by default. I haven’t met you, but I am sure you are a friend, until and unless you prove otherwise.

And I would really appreciate it if you wouldn’t prove otherwise.

But this attitude was hard-won, not discovered in a sudden stroke of coolness. It’s been over 20 years — uh-oh, am I bragging? — and it’s taken a long time to make peace with my identity both as an individual and as part of the greater foreigner-in-Mexico population. I don’t know if it’s my time here or just my age. Maybe it was a really good mushroom trip. But I just refuse to get worked up: if you want to be friends, we’re friends. I’ll try to help you if you need help. If you don’t like me, then, oh well. I guess we’re not friends.

The comment section of this humor piece I wrote made the “not friends” column abundantly clear; self-sorting, even.

And it got me thinking: is online communication among us all helping or hurting? After all, no one would be as nasty to people’s faces as we might be online. Online, we’re anonymous; we could be anyone; and we can’t get punched in the face for being rude as hell.

A polarized society, at home and abroad

Perhaps it’s a reflection as well of the general polarity we find in the United States. I’m certainly not immune from self-sorting, of course: finding common ground with friends who are openly enthusiastic about a felon president is not always easy. In any case, everyone has strong opinions either way.

Yes, we foreigners are a varied bunch, each of us as unique as a snowflake. Complicating matters is the fact that the average U.S. or Canadian citizen is not someone who would voluntarily move to Mexico. Right off the bat, then, you’re dealing with someone whose type you might not be too familiar with.

Overall, the most even-keeled people I’ve met have been retirees, though this isn’t a hard and fast rule. You can be a weirdo at any age!

People closer to my own age are a bit of a mixed bag, though, and I’ve had a few relationships with other paisanos end abruptly at this point. This has only happened once with a Mexican friend, a neighbor who blocked me after I friended her husband, who I thought was also my friend, on Facebook. Given the demographics, I’d say the number of times it’s happened with those from my own culture makes it conspicuously likely.

Abrupt endings to friendships

The first cut off was by a couple from the U.S. who wanted help translating and getting paperwork done upon arrival. We’d had some great conversations online beforehand, but in real life, our chemistry was pretty tense and weird. No matter; they were paying me for my help, and I was going to do whatever I could to make it worth it. Mostly, it was fine.

But then there was a misunderstanding about what exactly was being charged, and I suddenly found myself buried under some very intense, urgent messages. I gifted them some extra live interpretation time as a sign of goodwill and thought we were fine. Later, though, when I wanted to send a message to see how their house hunting had gone, I realized I’d been blocked on WhatsApp and Facebook.

Since then, I’ve found I’m not the only person to have received that treatment. A clear picture of kookiness has emerged, so I guess it’s not just me. The experience did convince me, however, that I definitely did not want to make a career of helping people settle down here.

Another cut-off came from someone who’d been a friend and mentor to me for over 20 years. That one was completely unexpected, and it hurt. I’d excused myself from what I saw as a minor favor, an action which my friend apparently interpreted as a sign of deep disrespect. I was oblivious that he was upset with me, and only learned that he was months later from another friend. By the time I wrote him to apologize, that was it. I never heard from him again.

The last incident was quite recent, with a friend of three years. I thought we were really close, but when I unwisely hounded her about getting her dog fixed so it wouldn’t get all the dogs in the neighborhood pregnant, that was it, too. I was asked to leave her house immediately, even though home was over three hours away.

Keeping an open mind on other expats

What is with these gringos and abruptly cutting people off? Mexicans may have a reputation for being dramatic, but my relationships with them have gone through rocky patches and come out just fine. Only my own paisanos have been so mad that they banished me from their lives. Is it something about North Americans, or is it just something about North Americans who live in Mexico? I will probably never know.

But I have not sworn off other U.S. Americans. Currently, we have a small breakfast group of foreigners in Xalapa that meets once a month. We share a nice meal and chat. We wouldn’t all necessarily be best friends were we in the U.S.

But this is different. When you’re in a foreign country without family, it’s nice to know people who know your culture and language on a native level. Real friendships, I still believe and have proven, are possible.

But for people who I know will definitely still be my friend even if I berate them about their unsterilized pets, I’m sticking with Mexicans.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/
