World.title: Breast milk shows benefit against antibiotic resistance
World.content:
Breast milk may offer babies a new health benefit: helping to limit the presence of antibiotic resistance genes in their gut. That is the conclusion of an international study led by Spain's National Research Council (CSIC), which has examined how certain components of human milk influence the bacteria that colonise the gut during the first months of life.

 

The study, published in "Cell Reports Medicine (source in Spanish)", finds that exclusive breastfeeding is associated with a lower abundance and diversity of antimicrobial resistance genes in babies' intestines.

"Promoting breastfeeding appears to be an effective strategy for reducing antimicrobial resistance genes present in intestinal bacterial communities during a critical stage in the development of the microbiota", explains M. Carmen Collado, a CSIC researcher at the Institute of Agrochemistry and Food Technology (IATA).

How does breast milk influence antibiotic resistance?

One of the keys lies in human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), molecules that occur naturally in breast milk which babies do not digest directly, but which serve as food for certain beneficial gut bacteria and help maintain a balanced microbiota.

The researchers have found that some of these components are associated with a lower presence of certain genes conferring resistance to antibiotics.

"HMOs act as ecological modulators of the gut microbiota: they promote the growth of microorganisms capable of using them and may limit the spread of bacteria carrying specific resistance genes", says Collado.

To reach these conclusions, the researchers analysed faecal samples from 57 one-month-old babies in Valencia, along with milk samples from their mothers. The results were later validated with data from another 199 breastfed babies in the Netherlands.

Mode of delivery also plays a role

The study notes that both the mode of delivery and feeding are decisive factors in the composition of the intestinal resistome, that is, the collection of antimicrobial resistance genes present in gut bacteria.

The researchers found differences in the diversity of these genes between babies born by caesarean section and those born by vaginal delivery, while exclusive breastfeeding was associated with a lower abundance and diversity of resistance genes.

"The first months of life represent a critical window in which the gut microbiota is being established and in which different environmental factors, such as mode of delivery or feeding, can leave a lasting imprint", explains Anna Samarra, a researcher trained at IATA-CSIC and now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of California, San Diego.

World.title: War is likely to drag on into winter according to Zelenskyy following talks with US envoys
World.content:
Following talks held on Sunday between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his team and US peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in Ukraine's capital of Kyiv, the Ukrainian President said that war with Russia "at the moment" is likely to continue into winter.

 

"We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter -- and this is how it appears at the moment." Zelenskyy said.

Witkoff added that comprise would be needed to be seen from both side.

It was Witkoff and Kushner's first time travelling to Kyiv, who gave positive feedback of the talks however lacked to announce any breakthroughs on ending the war with Russia.

"We think we have the ingredients to get to that place," he said.

"We've had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes."

Kushner added, "Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we've learned a lot from the trip."

Meanwhile, according to Zelenskyy more talks with British, German and French representatives were still ongoing.

Earlier in the day Zelenskyy had said "We are expecting one session of our talks, and then another session will be held with the European NSAs (national security advisors)."

The Ukrainian President noted that he was grateful for the presence of European partners, "Here we are all on the same side." he said.

One day before, Witkoff, who is US President Trump's business ally, and Kushner who is Trump's son in law had travelled to Moscow to meet with Russia's President Vladimir Putin.

They then arrived to Kyiv in the same way as all the other delegations, by train, with "Peace Express" written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station. Though Zelenskyy said "everything" had been prepared "to make our airports operational", but Russian strikes ruled out that option.

Both Putin and Zelenskyy have vowed not to launch strikes on Moscow and Kyiv during whilst the US envoys hold talks.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since 2022 when Russia launched it's full scale invasion of Ukraine.

Previously in Moscow

In a statement a White House official said that in Moscow envoys had "discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks".

Meanwhile, the Kremlin said the Americans "put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement", without saying more.

Strikes on Ukraine have increased this summer while Putin has repeatedly said that Moscow wants to occupy the rest of eastern Ukraine.

World.title: IFA 2026: Xiaomi wants its smart-home cars on European roads by 2027
World.content:
Xiaomi may still be best known for its smartphones. But at IFA 2026, the Chinese technology company presented plans for a future that no longer fits inside people's pockets.

 

Home appliances and connected devices have become an increasingly important part of its business. Now, Xiaomi is putting greater emphasis on four wheels — and the shift is hard to miss at IFA.

Inside the company's exhibition space in Berlin, one of the first things visitors encounter is a futuristic-looking car carrying the familiar Xiaomi logo, but on a very different scale.

Xiaomi cars are already a familiar sight for consumers in China. Now the company wants to bring them to European roads too.

In that spirit, Xiaomi announced at IFA 2026 that it plans to launch its electric vehicles in Europe in 2027, marking the next stage of its expansion beyond smartphones and consumer electronics.

Xiaomi has also expanded its range of home appliances and connected devices. Euronews

But simply selling cars is not the company's ultimate goal. Like many of the technology companies exhibiting in Berlin, Xiaomi is increasingly focused on connecting different parts of everyday life.

It calls its approach "Human x Car x Home", an ecosystem designed to link personal devices, the car and technology around the home. In practice, the idea is to let you steer your home from behind the wheel of your car.

Euronews took a closer look at Xiaomi's vision at IFA 2026 to see how that ecosystem is supposed to work.

'Human x Car x Home': The vision

Rather than treating the car as a separate product, Xiaomi wants to integrate it into the same connected system that already links devices around the home. The aim is for users to move between different environments while staying connected to the devices they rely on every day.

Euronews At IFA, Xiaomi presented its "Human × Car × Home" ecosystem, connecting cars, smartphones and home devices.

At IFA, Xiaomi demonstrated what that could look like in practice. From inside the car, users could control devices back at home, including opening and closing connected curtains and switching the air conditioning on or off.

This means the car could effectively become another control point for the smart home. Someone leaving work, for example, could adjust the air conditioning before arriving home, while other connected devices could be controlled directly from the vehicle.

Xiaomi says AI and its HyperOS operating system are intended to provide the technological link between these devices. Its longer-term vision goes beyond users manually controlling individual appliances, with AI eventually using contextual information to coordinate devices across the car, smartphone and home.

For Xiaomi, the car is therefore not only a new product category, but another part of a wider connected ecosystem — extending its technology beyond smartphones and the home and onto the road.

Alongside its more concrete plans, Xiaomi has also left room for imagination, exploring what could become possible further down the road.

Xiaomi's Vision Gran Turismo Euronews

Among the concepts presented at IFA is the Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo. The electric hypercar concept was developed for the Gran Turismo racing game series and explores ideas around design, aerodynamics and digital interaction.

For now, however, this vehicle remains firmly a concept rather than a preview of a production model expected to hit the road any time soon.

Local partners

But despite leaving room for experimentation, Xiaomi also made clear that its European ambitions go beyond concepts. At its IFA press conference on 3 September, the company took concrete steps towards its planned market entry.

During a signing ceremony, the company signed letters of intent with eight German automotive retail groups: Emil Frey Germany, the Ernst Dello Group, Autohaus Dinnebier, Hahn Automobile, the LUEG Mobility Group, Fett & Wirtz, SPT Avior and Penske-Jacobs.

Germany, however, is only intended to be the starting point, with Xiaomi planning similar partnerships in other European markets.

"Europe is a key market for our global strategy," Xiaomi Chief Marketing Officer Xu Fei said during the press conference.

The company is also planning significant investment to support this broader strategy. Between 2026 and 2030, Xiaomi says it intends to invest more than €24 billion globally in research and development, with a focus on areas including AI, operating systems, semiconductors, intelligent vehicles, robotics and smart manufacturing.

World.title: Report of suspected attack on baby dolphin in Ceuta area where migrants are staying
World.content:
A bottlenose dolphin calf was found dead at around midday on Wednesday on Trampolín beach in Ceuta, according to 'El Faro de Ceuta', and in circumstances that the Association for the Defence of Urban Trees, Biodiversity and the Environment (DAUBMA) considers an attack. The organisation has filed a formal complaint with the Guardia Civil and requested that proceedings be opened to clarify what happened.

 

According to the association's account, the animal reached the shore alive, disoriented, possibly because of the fog in the area that morning. Once on land, DAUBMA says, several people dragged it out of the water and hit it on the head with a stick.

The organisation says it has photographs, videos and social media screenshots that also show blood beneath one of the animal’s eyes, as well as some of the people present trying to wipe it away. In its view, this points to a direct attack and to manipulation of the carcass that is incompatible with any attempt to help the animal. All of this material has been made available to the Guardia Civil.

A verified video that circulated widely, with no perpetrators identified

The footage, first shared on social media, was recorded on the part of the beach where people who entered Ceuta during the mass crossing on 30 and 31 July remain camped.

A worker from the cleaning company Ecoservicios, who was in the area, witnessed the scene and warned those present that they should stop what they were doing and call an environmental collection service.

After that warning, according to witnesses, they tried to return the animal to the sea, although it was no longer showing any signs of life. So far there has been no formal identification of those responsible: that is precisely what DAUBMA is seeking with its complaint to the Guardia Civil.

The case has sparked outrage online, and a local resident, Nadia García Gómez, has launched a petition on change.org calling for those responsible to be identified.

García Gómez stresses that she does not belong to any association and argues for a firm response to animal abuse: "This cruel act must be tried and punished", she wrote online, in which she asks the authorities "to do something about it". The petition points out that the bottlenose dolphin is a strictly protected species in the EU and that injuring or killing an individual can constitute a criminal offence.

DAUBMA and CECAM respond to criticism

Responding to those who ask where animal rights associations are when dead wildlife is found in Ceuta, DAUBMA and CECAM say their work focuses on documenting cases and passing them on to institutions, while lamenting the lack of any response.

They explain that more than three months ago they submitted to the Government Delegation a dossier on other cases of dead or affected animals, including dolphins and turtles showing, they say, signs of having fallen victim to drift nets, which are banned in the EU, but have received no reply.

They add that an attempt to file a complaint with Seprona was initially not processed, so they went to the duty court with technical and graphic material; the court, according to their account, ordered the case to be provisionally closed pending a Seprona report that has still not arrived.

Both organisations say they coordinate with emergency services, the Guardia Civil, Semar and collection companies, and call on the authorities to ensure that wildlife protection does not remain mere rhetoric.

World.title: Mediterranean Sea now at spa temperature, daily average 28.54°C on 13 August
World.content:
Surface waters across the Mediterranean Sea reached an average temperature of 28.54ºC on 13 August, the highest recorded since at least 1940, Spain's State Meteorological Agency reported on Sunday.

 

Aemet itself noted on social media that throughout almost the whole of August the sea was breaking daily temperature records, one after another, with barely any respite.

The warning comes just weeks after Mercator Ocean International, which implements the Copernicus marine service, confirmed that July had already been the hottest month ever measured in the Mediterranean. The average that month was 27.07ºC, with a margin of uncertainty of ±0.27ºC, beating the previous maximum, set in July 2025 (26.68ºC), by four tenths of a degree.

Mercator Ocean's comparison series begins in 1993, meaning that both bodies, despite using different methods and reference periods, concur in describing a sea that has entered a thermal regime not seen before.

Daily average sea temperature in the Mediterranean, 2026 Aemet

This pattern has been in place for months

Data from late June were already pointing that way. Aemet (source in Spanish) warned at the time that Mediterranean temperatures had reached levels more typical of the second half of August, when the sea is usually at its warmest.

At the start of the summer, temperatures rose to 2.6ºC above normal, to the point that the sea exceeded the average usually seen in mid-August while it was still June, an anomaly the agency itself described as exceptional.

On a planetary scale, the phenomenon is not confined to the Mediterranean. July 2026 was the month with the highest global ocean surface temperature in the entire record, with an average of 21ºC between 60º north and 60º south.

Across the Mediterranean basin, 27% of the sea experienced its warmest July since 1993 and around 70% of the surface ranked among the four hottest Julys ever measured, ruling out the idea that the record can be explained by just a few exceptional locations.

It is important to stress that the sea-temperature record cannot be singled out as the direct cause of the high temperatures recorded on land, as many different factors come into play in the atmosphere. It can, however, alter conditions along the coast: water releases heat more slowly than the land surface, so a Mediterranean this warm makes it harder for temperatures to fall at night, increases humidity and leads to hotter nights near the shore.

The build-up of energy in the sea also affects ecosystems. Prolonged marine heatwaves subject organisms adapted to specific thermal ranges to considerable stress and can alter species distribution, increase mortality and change the functioning of entire coastal communities.

With the figure recorded on 13 August, the Mediterranean has once again surpassed the record it had set only a few weeks earlier, in a summer which, on land and at sea, keeps breaking its own records.

World.title: EU chief von der Leyen heads to Greenland in show of support for the island
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is visiting Greenland on Sunday and Monday as the bloc signals its continued support for the island amid US President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire it.

 

As part of the visit, von der Leyen is expected to sign a joint declaration between the EU and the Danish autonomous territory on Monday.

Since his return to the White House in January last year, Trump has claimed the US needs to take control of Greenland for its "national security," arguing that either China or Russia would otherwise seize the island.

Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa issued a joint statement in January in which they highlighted the importance of "territorial integrity and sovereignty" and said the EU stood "in full solidarity with Denmark and the people of Greenland."

Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos this year, von der Leyen said the EU was also working on a "massive European investment surge" in Greenland in a bid to ramp up Arctic security.

The Commission has proposed allocating €530 million to Greenland under its budget for the 2028–2034 period, which it said reflected its "growing geostrategic importance in the Arctic."

The Financial Times reported that von der Leyen is set to announce an additional €200 million in funding for the island during her visit.

Houses are seen near the coast of a sea inlet of Nuuk, Greenland, on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

In May, Trump's special envoy to Greenland, Jeff Landry, said it was time the US "puts its footprint back" on the territory.

Landry, who is also the governor of Louisiana, made the comments during a trip to the territory, his first since his appointment to the special envoy role in December 2025.

Speaking from Greenland's capital, Nuuk, Landry told Agence France-Presse: "I think that you're seeing the president talk about increasing national security operations and repopulating certain bases in Greenland."

"Everyone that I've talked to in Greenland would love to see the US repopulate those bases," he continued, adding that the territory "needs the US."

In January, the leaders of five political parties in Greenland’s parliament released a joint statement with a clear message to the US.

"We do not want to be Americans, we do not want to be Danes; we want to be Greenlanders," it read.

The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and more than 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War. It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.

Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, according to the US Space Force.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: AfD wants to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt — but how?
World.content:
Following its record-breaking success in the state election, the far-right AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is aiming to form a government.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in this eastern German state quite difficult.

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund announced on public broadcaster ARD: "As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround." At the same time, he acknowledged that there are currently no political parties that he considers suitable for a coalition government.

Above all, he was referring to the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds power in coalitions both in Saxony-Anhalt and on the federal level in Germany. Siegmund, along with the entire AfD leadership, has characterized the CDU's policy of refusing to work with the AfD a failure.

On public broadcaster ZDF, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel sharply criticized the CDU for stonewalling the AfD: "The CDU will not win another election — not a federal election. And this clearly gives the AfD a mandate to govern. Because we are democrats, we do not refuse to work with others."

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me." Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.

The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: it has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an ARD interview that these issues are non-negotiable.

Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.

AfD: Saxony-Anhalt result will 'shake all of Germany' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel told ZDF television: "Who ultimately forms the government — perhaps through a tolerance agreement or even a coalition — remains to be seen."

On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."

Will the BSW decide on the government of Saxony-Anhalt?

The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), should it manage to move into the state parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

Take, for example, Oliver Kirchner, co-chair of the AfD caucus in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt: "If we end up behind the lectern as the opposition, it will be brutal for the others," he warned during an AfD livestream.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
World.content:
With well over 40% for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Saxony-Anhalt has witnessed a landmark election night. DW's reporters were on the ground.

After an unusually quiet evening at the press center for the Saxony-Anhalt state election, journalists, camera crews and technicians were suddenly running around, jostling and shouting. Ulrich Siegmund, the leading candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), went running off with his bodyguards, looking for the best place to stand so that he would be clearly visible on camera when the election projections started appearing on the screens.

And then, a few minutes later, the commotion started up again, as AfD party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla arrived, beaming just as broadly as Siegmund. Another scramble ensued, and the bodyguards shouted: "Stay back!"

At 6 pm, when the preliminary results finally came in, the AfD was well above 40%. For the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which governs the region between the Elbe and the Harz Mountains, it is a nightmare — there's no other way to put it. Weidel subsequently declares the result a clear mandate for her party to form a government. It's hard to disagree with her on that. She tells reporters that even before Christmas rolls around, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) will be replaced following this election result.

Weidel: 'This is a mandate for us to form a government!'

After all, Merz, whose popularity has hit record lows across the country, was rarely seen during this election campaign. And his party here in Saxony-Anhalt was glad about that.

AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla also spoke of a blow to the chancellor, who he said only makes grandiose announcements. He also accused the chancellor of "unnecessarily escalating" tensions with Russia recently. Once the cameras were off, Chrupalla admitted that even he hadn't expected such a clear victory.

The AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed far-right extremist," held its election party at the Altes Theater, just a stone's throw from the press center. Before entering the building, journalists and visitors were searched by police dogs, and bags were checked twice.

"This feels less like a state election and more like a G7 summit," said DW correspondent Matthew Moore, after finally getting into the Altes Theater. To maintain order over the weekend, 1,800 additional police officers were dispatched to Saxony-Anhalt from other federal states.

'Like a trip to the dentist': The CDU at the Maritim Hotel

And what about the CDU, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for the last 24 years? The voters' rejection of the party could hardly be more decisive. That Sven Schulze, the incumbent premier, did not resign immediately could even be seen as an act of bravery. With a stony expression, he told his supporters: "This is democracy!"

At the beginning of the year, Schulze succeeded Reiner Haseloff as head of government in Saxony-Anhalt. Seventy-two-year-old Haseloff was highly respected in the state and yet did not wish to run for another term. But when he stepped down, it was too late for Schulze to counter the force of support for the AfD.

The CDU election party — which turned out to be not much of a party at all — was held at the four-star Maritim Hotel. In the hotel ballroom, only die-hard CDU supporters remained to witness the debacle. This year's results were half of what they were in the previous state election. It was a difficult defeat for the party that remained the strongest political force in Saxony-Anhalt for the last twenty years. "It's a bit like being in the dentist's waiting room," a CDU supporter told DW reporter Bernd Riegert with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."

Uncertainty regarding the BSW

No matter how big the right-wing populists' election victory may be, the AfD has little chance of governing with an absolute majority. And so far, all other parties have ruled out entering into a coalition with it.

It will likely come down to the economically left-wing and politically conservative Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which could narrowly make it into the state parliament.

Meanwhile, Eva von Angern, the leading candidate for the socialist Left Party in Saxony-Anhalt, spoke of a "dark day" for the state, because of "the consequences this result could have for Saxony-Anhalt and the people of Saxony-Anhalt." And by that, she was also referring to the AfD's hardline policy toward refugees. During the campaign, the AfD made it clear time and again that asylum seekers whose applications were rejected would be deported on a large scale "from day one."

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hope within the SPD for a majority without the AfD

As for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Chancellor Merz's federal government struck a surprisingly optimistic tone. Despite predictions that they would fare much worse, the Social Democrats are now assured of representation in the state parliament. In distant Berlin, SPD Secretary-General Tim Klüssendorf was not yet ready to give up hope that a coalition of all mainstream parties might be able to bypass the AfD and form a coalition: "If such a majority exists, then it should be formed with the participation of all the parties represented in this state parliament," he said.

Greens between euphoria and shock

The environmentalist Greens spent election night somewhere between euphoria and shock. Actually, the party should be delighted with such an unexpected result. Predictions had long suggested they might fail to clear the five-percent threshold, but now they're safely in. DW reporter Giula Saudelli said that some staff members at the Green Party's election party had tears in their eyes when the projections appeared on the screens: tears of relief for their own party and tears of shock at the AfD's gains.

"There's no reason to jump for joy when it's still unclear whether far-right extremists will be able to govern this state," party co-leader Felix Banaszak told DW. He had spent a lot of time campaigning in Saxony-Anhalt. Videos on social media showed him being openly attacked and verbally abused. But he continued nonetheless. People close to him say that this may have contributed to the Greens' election success — a success that doesn't quite feel like one.

… and in Berlin, the chancellor remains silent

But this much is clear: it was an historic evening in Saxony-Anhalt: a defining moment. Much remains unclear, such as who will eventually govern the state and what consequences this will have for Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A press conference has been scheduled with him for midday on Monday.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.

On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.

In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.

DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.

Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.

Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."

The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.

Verdict: False

There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.

The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.

Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.

Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system

Though a false claim purported that AfD ballots were destroyed, the AfD in fact won a huge share of the vote on Sunday Image: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.

"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.

Verdict: False

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.

The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.

Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".

One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.

"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.

Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections

A misleading claim alleged that postal ballots were being counted before polls closed Image: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

Did Halle start counting ballots too early?

Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.

Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".

Verdict: Misleading

The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.

Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.

The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."

The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
World.content:
The election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government. Pollsters point to dissatisfaction with Chancellor Merz as one reason for his party's poor showing.

Only 1.6 million eligible voters were called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, September 6. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

For weeks it was clear that the vote had become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

The in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the election, doubling its percentage compared to the last election five years ago, while the ruling CDU lost half of its support. If the AfD now manages to form a government, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.

A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?

Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW before the election. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

Koschmieder also predicted that a strong showing by the AfD would intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist. The CDU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Most analysts believe that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party.

Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.

But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.

SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

What about the Social Democrats? They have remained at around 8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt. This is a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.

World.title: Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
World.content:
Ahead of Germany's state elections in September, rumors began circulating on social media claiming that postal voting is not secure — claims that have also been made about other elections. Here's why they're wrong.

Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. Saxony-Anhalt was first and voters handed a strong result to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization" , could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections . But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.

DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.

Does postal voting manipulate election results?

Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.

This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok , X and Facebook .

Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.

Social media is rife with posts like this one on X, which cited individual problems with mail-in ballots as evidence that postal voting is fundamentally unreliable Image: X/AfD

DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.

The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau , where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.

Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria , a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.

There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.

But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.

The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.

"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."

In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund has called for postal voting to be restricted to justified exceptional cases. But officials have defended postal voting as a secure and established procedure Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

Postal voting easy to manipulate?

Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.

"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14.

Some posts have argued that postal votes are easier to manipulate during the counting process Image: X

This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire , for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control."

DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.

Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.

That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.

In Germany, eligible voters can be called upon by local authorities to serve as election workers and are generally required by law to accept the role Image: ABBfoto/picture alliance

In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.

DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.

DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.

A familiar claim beyond Germany

The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.

During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.

Fact-check: The truth on burned votes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.

"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.

He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.

"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.

This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check. It was first published on September 4, and updated and republished on September 6.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
World.content:
The AfD has emerged as the strongest party in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt by a wide margin. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage.

Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is also home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still accounts for around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the Elbe River, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.

Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, international attention is now turning to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government after the Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, won in a landslide on September 6.

Can the AfD rule the state?

The far-right AfD has taken a massive lead at the Saxony-Anhalt election, but it was not immediately clear if it will be able to form government. The party's state leader said the result sends "a signal to Berlin." The ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since German reunification in 1990, has lost half of its support. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) which has failed to secure representation by falling underneath the threshhold of 5%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution has classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt was also at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party.

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.

What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in the state feel with developments in Germany. Many jobs disappeared in the years following reunification, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt also faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the state's Statistical Office, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.

What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the success of the far-right DVU some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.

Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of the Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded.

"I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely," he said. In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script," he said.

The new parliament will convene on October 6, the weeks leading up to this date will see difficult negotiations to form a majority for a new government.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 24, and updated following the election on September 6.

World.title: Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce
World.content:
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun has appealed to the international community to "take immediate action to stop these violations" of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon.

At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on Lebanon on Sunday, which comes despite a ceasefire between the two countries, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.

The Lebanese officials also said around 20 other people, including children, were wounded in the strikes.

The office of Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" that targeted "purely civilian administrations and health centers."

"President Aoun held the Israeli side fully responsible for this ongoing escalation, calling on the United States and the international community to take immediate action to stop ​these violations and hold the perpetrators accountable," his aides said in a statement.

In turn, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the strikes were a response to "a blatant violation" by Hezbollah militants.

"Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon," the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.

What do we know about the strikes?

Early on Sunday morning, the Israeli military issued an online evacuation alert for Arab Salim, saying it identified a "Hezbollah facility" there.

Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building mentioned in the original evacuation warning.

NNA also reported that "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it." Two women were killed in the strike.

Two women were reportedly killed by Israeli strikes on Arab Salim village Image: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

Another two people were killed in Israeli strikes near the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which lies on the edge of Israel's "security zone" that it occupies in southern Lebanon.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said an Israeli strike "totally destroyed" a disused hospital. The Health Ministry called the incident "another grave violation of international humanitarian law."

The Israeli military said its targets included what it described as a Hezbollah command center inside a building that was previously used as a hospital, as well as a weapons depot.

"The strikes were carried out in response to Hezbollah’s attempted attack yesterday in the Ali Taher Ridge area and to remove threats posed by Hezbollah," it said.
