World.title: Tree-killing beetle still poses major threat, as bird flu takes centre stage
World.content:
It was only a couple of years ago when everyone was talking about a tiny but deadly invasive beetle that could wipe out Perth's tree canopy and wreak havoc in agriculture and native forests.

People were on high alert for signs of the polyphagous shot-hole borer and distressed when beautiful big trees in Kings Park and Hyde Park had to be chopped down to stop the spread.

A quarantine zone was placed around the metropolitan area as part of a national response to the pest, and when eradication failed, the response shifted to a long-term management plan.

The invasive pest has destroyed multiple trees in Perth's Hyde Park. (ABC News: Nicholas Martyr)

But now it seems to have gone quiet.

In fact, it is more that another deadly biosecurity threat has grabbed our attention, the H5N1 bird flu.

Eradication of shot-hole borer from WA not possible Authorities say eradicating the shot-hole borer pest, which has devastated Perth's tree canopy, is not feasible.

People are being told to keep their eyes peeled for sick birds and wildlife and quickly report to authorities.

In the background, shot-hole borers, which burrow into trees with devastating consequences, are still crawling, flying and looking for new hosts to chew on.

Measuring just 1 to 2 millimetres, the beetles were detected for the first time in an avocado orchard in the Perth suburb of Carabooda in December.

The softer wood of the avocado trees makes them particularly susceptible to the borer, with crops in other countries devastated by the pest.

The soft trunks of avocado trees are particularly susceptible to the shot-hole borer. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

That makes the south-west of WA the new front line.

It is where more than 51,000 of the 131,000 tonnes of avocados grown around Australia were produced last financial year, according to Avocados Australia.

Beetle poses 'real threat'

Manjimup avocado grower and WA director of Avocados Australia Brad Rodgers said there had been no signs of the beetle in the region so far.

Brad Rodgers says farmers are regularly checking their crops for the pest. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

"It's a real threat and it's a real concern to farmers," he said.

"It's very critical for our livelihood and for us to grow the fruit that Australians and West Australians love. We would like to contain it if we can."

He and other farmers regularly check their crops, and the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development is helping with information and advice on pruning to manage the borer.

Under the microscope

The department is also involved in a research project with Murdoch University studying Australia's only laboratory colony of shot-hole borers.

Wei Xu is studying what attracts and repels the borer. (Supplied)

The team is led by Wei Xu, who showed the ABC a series of test tubes filled with sawdust from different trees, while pointing out the tunnels made by the borers.

"They build the gallery so they can grow fungi. There are some insects inside," Dr Xu said.

They are studying what repels the borer but also what attracts them.

"Then we can use that in the trap for example to monitor their population in the field, to detect them or to trap and kill them," he said.

A research project at Murdoch University is studying Australia's only laboratory colony of shot-hole borers. (ABC News: Nicolas Perpitch)

He said early detection was the key to stopping the spread out of the Perth quarantine zone and potentially to the rest of the country, especially northern regions of the east coast where the borers would thrive in the warmer, more humid conditions.

"So they may amplify quickly and spread quickly and that would be a big threat to the whole of Australia," he said.

Overshadowed by bird flu

But there are concerns bird flu is taking the community's attention and government resources away from shot-hole borer.

"One of the concerns we have at present is that we're facing a bird flu crisis, which is going to take up an awful lot of biosecurity resources, including people in government," Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said.

"When we lose that focus that's potentially a really good opportunity for this beetle to really spread and start causing damage in other parts of Australia," Dr Booth said.

The tiny pest has led to the destruction of thousands of trees across Perth. (Supplied: Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development)

But the WA government insisted its surveillance and management programs of the borer had not changed.

"There has been no change to Western Australia's polyphagous shot-hole borer response as a result of the government's response to H5 bird flu," a government spokesperson said.

That included quarantine controls, surveillance, regulation, training and "capacity building to slow the spread and manage the impact of shot-hole borer".

World.title: AI replacing Auslan interpreter jobs in regional towns
World.content:
For Australia's deaf and hearing-impaired community, finding and booking an in-person Auslan interpreter can be difficult.

In an attempt to fill the void, virtual services, apps and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being used to bring translation services to regions that struggled to find them in the past.

But the move is having an unintended side effect, as the few registered Auslan interpreters living and working in regional areas say they are suddenly finding themselves out of work.

Interpreter Cindy Murray quit her job earlier this year.

"The demand [for in-person Auslan interpreters] has always been there, and especially for rural and regional people," Ms Murray said.

But she said agencies were unwilling to pay travel costs and were reluctant to prioritise in-person interpreters over virtual ones.

Cindy Murray was one of the few registered Auslan interpreters living and working in regional Victoria. (Supplied: Cindy Murray)

One agency told Ms Murray there were no jobs in regional areas, despite deaf clients telling her when they tried to book an interpreter, the same agency would tell them there was nobody available, and then offer a virtual interpreter or live captioning instead.

Live captioning is a form of AI software that records and writes out spoken conversations in real time to help users with hearing impairments access these conversations.

It does not include translating responses from Auslan to spoken language, which is why captioning is not always appropriate.

Virtual interpreters can work remotely, appearing on a screen to translate what they hear via a live feed, and often working at a lower cost than in-person translators.

Ms Murray said having options was good but the effect on interpreters was not.

"I think the lack of interpreters will continue to get worse and worse because of the way we're treated," Ms Murray said.

"There are some people who like AI. I mean — knock yourself out — if it translates, that's great.

" But there's a lot of people who don't [like AI]. They want a face-to-face experience. "

A changing landscape

Brent Phillips is the chief services officer for Deaf Connect, a nationwide Auslan service provider and social impact organisation working with deaf and hearing-impaired people.

Mr Philips said his organisation prioritised "preference of the customer".

Brent Phillips says AI will never be a replacement for interpreting. (Supplied: Brent Phillips)

"If a customer's first preference is an in-person interpreter then we do everything possible to provide one," he said.

When one is not available, Mr Phillips said his company worked closely with the customer to find a work-around.

He said the advent of AI was definitely changing the Auslan interpretation landscape.

"We're keeping a very close eye on what's happening in the AI space and we are actively influencing and advising the design of future AI sign-language products," Mr Phillips said.

" But our strong opinion is it will never be a replacement for interpreting. "

Interpreters on demand

Deaf Victoria regional outreach officer Gary Kerridge said the lack of in-person Auslan interpreters was a widespread issue.

"Unfortunately, demand for [interpreters] is very high and they are often booked out," he said.

Gary Kerridge has more than 40 years' experience working in the disability and deafness sector. (Supplied: Gary Kerridge/Deaf Victoria)

Mr Kerridge, who is deaf and lives in a regional community, said using AI and virtual interpreting services was a way to combat the shortfall while also saving on potential costs to a participant's NDIS funding.

He helped implement a trial of an app called Convo, which was created by a deaf-owned and operated company in 2021.

It is a virtual interpreter app, allowing users to access an Auslan interpreter anywhere, any time, for a fee, and for qualified interpreters from anywhere in the country to sign up to work when they are available.

Ballarat City Council in regional Victoria is among the organisations trialling Convo.

Mr Kerridge said Convo still relied on human interpreters and was not intended to put face-to-face interpreters out of work.

"Sometimes [interpreting] can be done online, which reduces costs, but not all interpreting jobs are suitable to online," he said.

"The evidence shows this is a needed support, and I have no doubt that, rolled out properly, it will save lives."

World.title: Live: Wall Street slips as bond yields rise, ASX treading water
World.content:
The three key Wall Street indices slipped on Friday as key jobs data came in stronger than expected, heightening speculation the Fed will raise rates later this month.

S & P 500: -0.4%

-0.4% Dow: -0.5%

-0.5% Nasdaq: -0.3%

US non-farm payrolls rose by 162,000 jobs last month against a forecast 56,000 gain. July jobs numbers were also revised up to a gain of 21,000 from the previously reported drop of 23,000. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%.

Two-year yields, which are particularly sensitive to changes in monetary policy, led the rise in Treasuries and were last up 4 basis points at 4.37%.

The yield on 10-year Treasury notes was up nearly 2 basis points to about 4.78%.

"Good news for the economy, but not such good news for those hoping the Fed will sit tight at the 16 September board meeting," IG Markets Tony Sycamore said.

Futures traders on the ASX 200 couldn't decide if it was good or bad news and remained on the fence.

When the market closed on Saturday morning (AEST), a fall of 1 point, or 0.01%, was priced in.

The moves were more definitive on the oil markets. The global Brent and US WTI benchmarks rose again as missiles and drones continued to whiz about the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent futures: +0.8% to $US92.68/barrel

+0.8% to $US92.68/barrel WTI futures: +0.2% to $US91.48/barrel

Over the week, Brent rose 8%, while US crude gained 10%.

Reuters reported US diesel prices hit a record high leading into the weekend.

The rally in oil prices combined with a much steeper fuel price increase has pushed inflation and government borrowing costs higher around the world and intensified fears that global economic growth might pull back without some relief.

"All sectors of the economy are affected by diesel," Rystad Energy chief economist Claudio Galimberti told Reuters.

Oil prices may well take another step up today after US forces struck and disabled three Iranian oil tankers in response to Iran targeting two US warships with ballistic missiles.

The barrage was followed by a social media volley from US Admiral Brad Cooper.

Despite US Treasuries pushing the US dollar higher, the Aussie dollar was relatively unmoved and closed the week at 72.04 US cents, its highest weekly close in four months.

And gold slipped as the odds of a Fed hike in September shortened.

Copper posted its 10th consecutive week of gains and moved closer to its record high of $US14,527/tonne.

Iron ore also edged higher to just under $US100/tonne.

With Reuters

Labor frontbencher Mark Butler is rejecting claims the introduction of an opt-out algorithm amounts to censorship.

The government's digital duty of care legislation will be introduced to parliament later this week and is expected to create an opt-out system so users can turn off algorithms on social media.

But the Coalition is concerned the laws would hand the minister too much power to determine what is and is not online harm.

Speaking with ABC's Radio National Breakfast, Butler says the change is pretty "unremarkable" as he dismissed the opposition's claim.

"It's pretty unremarkable really to expect that big companies have a duty of care not to harm Australian citizens, particularly frankly young Australians," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

"You know, the idea is that this is some censorship or infringement of civil liberties almost harks back to the days of the 1970s when people were protesting about seatbelts being introduced to cars."

World.title: 'Not fair and quite sad': Cohort of workers being underpaid by billions
World.content:
International student Mai was full of pride when she landed her first job in Australia.

"At that time I was really happy because now I can live by myself, be more independent, not rely on my family and actually can afford the renting," the Australian National University student said.

But she said her employer at a Canberra hospitality business began to call her day and night, asking her to work at short notice, for which she was paid a flat rate below the minimum wage, even on weekends.

"Even sometimes when I saw my check-in and check-out sheet it was often rounded down, and I mean that's not fair and quite sad," Mai said.

"Everything was so hard to afford and even paying rent is now more difficult and you're actually working for a lot of hours but like your effort is not anywhere, it's not showing."

Mai is among the two-thirds of migrant workers who are paid less than they are owed under the Fair Work Act. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Mai, who has chosen that name to protect her identity, said she was "really afraid to speak up".

"And I was scared that my parents would be worried for me. So I would stay by myself, try to go get through all of it by myself," she said.

Passports taken, no breaks, threats

Associate Professor Bassina Farbenblum, who founded the Migrant Justice Institute, said the underpayment of temporary visa holders, such as in Mai's case, was often a clue that those businesses were committing other forms of exploitation.

She has co-authored a major study into migrant worker exploitation commissioned by the Commonwealth attorney-general's department, finding:

"International students alone may be short-changed by around $3.18 billion per year," the report said. "Not by accident, and not by a few rogue employers."

Associate Professor Bassina Farbenblum founded the Migrant Justice Institute which partners with UNSW Law. (ABC News: Simon Amery )

Associate Professor Farbenblum said they had found "that the more that people were underpaid, the more likely they experienced conditions like having their passport confiscated or being made to work very long hours with no breaks, often two weeks in a row".

"And in some cases threats of harm or violence," she said.

"One of the things we see, particularly for migrant workers, is a threat to report the worker to immigration if they speak up or if they do anything.

"They're really fearful of losing their visa and they need to pay for food and pay their rent."

Do you know more about this story? Email roy.tahlia@abc.net.au

How ABNs are used for exploitation

An ABN is a unique 11-digit number that identifies a business. (ABC News: Phil Jaiyawong)

Associate Professor Farbenblum said one of the biggest insights from the report, which heard from close to 10,000 migrant workers in Australia, was that cash-in-hand was no longer the preferred strategy to underpay employees on temporary visas.

"So we used to see that the way of keeping migrant workers off-the-books was to pay in cash. We're still seeing one in four paid at least some of their wages in cash, but what we're seeing now is increasing use of ABNs," she said.

" Then there's no record of these people as employees and their pay can't be compared against their entitlements under the Fair Work Act. "

ABN misclassification: An ABN is a unique 11-digit number that identifies a business.

More than one third of migrant workers in Australia are on ABNs.

of migrant workers in Australia are on ABNs. That is more than four times the rate of uptake in the general workforce.

Employers who deliberately misclassify employees are engaging in sham contracting.

Sham contracting sees employers evade paying basic employment entitlements like the minimum wage.

Workers can pursue exploitation claims

The Department of Home Affairs introduced a temporary visa in 2024 to allow people to remain in Australia for up to 12 months to pursue a workplace exploitation claim after their previous visa expired.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

The Commonwealth also has a Strengthening Reporting Protections Pilot which promises the Department of Home Affairs "will not cancel your visa if you have breached a work-related visa condition, and there is a link between that visa breach and workplace exploitation" that is reported.

But there are concerns very few temporary visa holders ever report workplace exploitation.

The ABC has asked the Department of Home Affairs what the uptake has been for its migrant worker protections but the department has not yet responded to the questions.

Mai said she believed almost no one came forward.

World.title: Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaAviation Five killed as Amazon plane overruns runway, hitting vehicles and bursting into flames Updated September 7, 2026 — 7:41am ,first published 6:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said. Three others were critically injured and two others taken to hospital with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference. Loading More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the crash, arriving to find the aircraft on fire as crews worked to extinguish the flames and assess patients. The Federal Aviation Administration said the aircraft overran the runway about 2pm on Sunday (Florida time) after heading into Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue officials said the plane struck multiple vehicles after leaving the runway.



Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was sending investigators and issued a full ground stop at Miami International – one of America’s busiest airports – as emergency crews responded. The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway, with two trucks parked nearby, according to images on social media. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire. An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday (Florida time). Getty Images Amazon confirmed that one of its planes – operated by US cargo carrier 21 Air – experienced an incident when it attempted to land in Miami. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson said in a post on X. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.”



Representatives for 21 Air, which began operating Boeing 767-300 freighters on behalf of Amazon in 2024, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24. The Amazon plane, which flew into Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, was being operated by 21 Air. Lynne Sladky All runways and taxiways were closed, an airport spokesperson said. About 250 flights were delayed at the airport as of late afternoon Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. The FAA warned that delays were likely to persist even after the airport reopened, with arrivals and departures expected to resume at a reduced rate.



The National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the crash. “We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a social media post. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.” AP, Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has described One Nation’s policy to allow voters access to 3 per cent of their superannuation contributions for three years as “nothing more than a headline”, as her party continues to coast behind Pauline Hanson’s party in the polls.

“This so far is nothing more than a headline. It hasn’t really been explained. Does the tax status of your superannuation, your discounted tax status, does that remain? So do you get a tax discount for paying your rent?” Hume asked on ABC television this morning.

“How does it affect your concessional caps? How does it affect your, you know, bring-forward provisions, carry-back provisions? How does it affect your superannuation balance at the end of the day? Are we turning our superannuation funds into banks? None of these questions have been answered.”

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer

According to a press release published on Hanson’s social media this morning, the 3 per cent payments would maintain the concessional tax treatment if they remained in a superannuation account.

“One Nation does have a habit of putting out a headline and putting out no details … I think that Australians should have the right to know exactly what this policy would mean for them,” Hume said.

In the most recent Resolve Political Monitor published by this masthead, the Coalition received 23 per cent of the primary vote, behind One Nation at 26 per cent. Labor was polling at 28 per cent.

World.title: Call to arms for Wests Tigers fans after another season slips by
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Call to arms for Wests Tigers fans after another season slips by Chris Barrett September 7, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fed up by years of dysfunction and disappointment, disgruntled Wests Tigers fans are set to push for the reinstatement of an independent board and a greater say in the direction of the under-performing club. The Tigers have missed the finals for the past 15 seasons – by far the longest dry spell of any team in the competition – and have only qualified for the play-offs three times since Balmain and Western Suburbs merged in 1999. Wests Tigers fans protest the removal of the club’s independent directors in December. Flavio Brancaleone With another underwhelming campaign now over, Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne has issued a call to arms for supporters to mobilise as part of a new independent group called Wests Tigers Unite to be formed in the off-season. “At the start of this season, Wests Tigers supporters deliberately held off establishing a permanent supporters’ organisation,” Byrne said. “Like every Tigers fan, we hoped the club had finally turned a corner and wanted to get behind the team.



“Regrettably, this season has shown the underlying problems remain unresolved. “After 15 years without finals football, Wests Tigers supporters have shown extraordinary loyalty. Yet they still have no meaningful say in the future of the club they love.” Tigers fans had reason to hope for better times earlier this year but they slipped two places from 13th to 15th. Flavio Brancaleone After a bright start to the year, the Tigers’ finals chances evaporated with eight losses in a row. Benji Marshall’s team was also at the centre of two of the biggest soap operas of the season: the signing of Jarome Luai by the PNG Chiefs and Adam Doueihi’s refusal to play against Canberra in July.



Off the field, questions continue to be asked about Tigers majority owners, the Holman Barnes Group, whose decades-old governance model places power over the $100 million licensed club operation in the hands of 20 so-called debenture holders. The only one of its kind remaining in the state, the debenture system has been the subject of an investigation by Liquor and Gaming NSW after multiple complaints were made about it. The Adam Doueihi saga was just another chapter in Wests Tigers’ slide in 2026. Getty Images HBG took over the Tigers board after it removed chairman Barry O’Farrell and three other independent directors in December in an intervention that prompted chief executive Shane Richardson to quit. The sacked directors were reinstated amid supporter protests and pressure from the NRL, but the owners restructured the board to give them effective control, scrapping the independent-led board after less than 12 months.



“When it all blew up in December, the undertaking was that Barry O’Farrell would be reinstated as chair and our understanding was an independent board would be reinstated, and that’s yet to occur,” said Gary Barnier, one of the architects of a 2023 governance review that led O’Farrell and other independents to briefly have the balance of power on the Tigers board. “The sooner it happens, the better we’ll all be. “Professional sporting organisations that are successful have professional governance and professional structures. Wests Tigers will benefit from putting those things in place.” After finishing 15th this season, down two spots from 2025, the new Tigers fan group aims to build on the movement that arose last year when the independent directors were unseated and seasoned operator Richardson left. Byrne said the administration and ownership of the Tigers remained unaccountable to fans and members “who have stuck by the club through thick and thin”.



“It’s no coincidence that the only time that the performance of the organisation has improved was in the period that an independent board was in place,” Byrne said. “Re-establishing that is a necessity for turning the club around. “Our goal is simple: to organise supporters, represent their views and advocate for governance arrangements that make the club more accountable to its members. “This is not about division. It’s about giving one of rugby league’s biggest and most passionate supporter bases the seat at the table it deserves.” It is yet to be determined what that looks like in practice, but there are myriad examples of supporters being able to exercise their will in Australian and world sport. In the NRL, members don’t have a say on club boards at most clubs any more, although they can still nominate and vote for directors of select teams, such as Canterbury and Penrith.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 V’landys v Gallop: The big-money brawl over Origin and finals In European soccer, supporters also have greater agency at member-owned clubs, such as Barcelona and Real Madrid, and in Germany’s Bundesliga, which mandates that members of a club hold at least 50 per cent of voting rights plus one vote. HBG has branched out into soccer recently, buying a stake in National Premier Leagues NSW team APIA Leichhardt and taking over the Central Coast Mariners in the A-League Women competition. Supporters will be able to register their interest in Wests Tigers Unite at the One Last Roar concert at Leichhardt Oval on September 19, which is being held before the venue is renovated. The iconic inner-west ground will be unavailable for games in 2027 while a $40 million upgrade takes place. The Tigers announced last week that they would play six home games at Campbelltown Stadium, as well as four at CommBank Stadium.

World.content:
One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce has said his party’s superannuation policy is about keeping Australians “in their home”, as he calls for workers to have more choice in how they access their retirement savings.

“We need to make sure in a cost of living crisis that we keep people in their home. What we are doing here is giving people back some of their own money from the future, not taking it out of their current balance, but some of their own money in the future. And what we have to realise that superannuation is not a national asset; it’s individuals’ asset,” Joyce told a Sydney press conference this morning.

Barnaby Joyce during a doorstop at Parliament House in Canberra. Dominic Lorrimer

“If you lose your house, as an accountant, you’re going to be vastly worse off than the benefit you’ll get from that margin of investment over the longer term. I just can’t see why the government’s got a problem with this,” Joyce said.

The policy would allow renters and mortgage holders to access 3 per cent of their compulsory superannuation contribution for three years and would be taxed at the concessional superannuation rate. The funds would be paid out by the superannuation funds, not employers.

“This is not a seismic shift in administration. It’s a change in attitude that if you’re doing it tough, you get some of your own money back,” Joyce said.

World.title: NRL finals schedule: Who plays who in week 1 and how the Warriors can make the Grand Final
World.content:
The Warriors had the minor premiership ripped from their grasp in the final match of the regular round, but now the club has its sights set on a maiden NRL premiership.

After 27 weeks, the NRL's top eight is locked in. Having sneaked into last years play-offs in seventh, the Penrith Panthers are back on top of the mountain.

Ivan Cleary's side needed to beat the Tigers by at least two points to secure the minor premiership, and romped home with a 38-10 win to emphatically claim it.

Going into the 27th and final round of the regular season, the Warriors were clear of the Panthers by just one on points differential, but were only able to scrape past Manly 31-30 to surrender the shield.

This leaves the Warriors in second spot on the ladder. They are joined by the Dolphins, Roosters, Sharks, Rabbitohs, Knights and Cowboys. So what will be the Warriors path to a first NRL crown?

The NRL finals system

Introduced in 2012 to replace to old McIntyre system, the format sees two teams eliminated in each of the first three weeks heading into the big dance.

Finishing in the top four offers a lifeline, with the teams given a second chance if they lose in the opening week.

Due to finishing second, the Warriors can win twice in the playoffs and reach the grand final.

The finals series is split into four weeks, the qualifiers/eliminators, the semi finals, the preliminary final, and of course, the grand final.

Penrith Panthers coach Ivan Cleary, pictured with son Nathan, is seeking to extend the side's dynasty in 2026. AAP/www.photosport.nz

In playoff footy, there is an unlimited period of golden point to find a winner. The Warriors will play their 23rd NRL playoff in their history next weekend, having qualified for the post season eleven times since 1995.

It will also be the sixth home final after previous contests against Canberra in 2002, Parramatta in 2007, the Sydney Roosters in 2008, Newcastle in 2023 and Penrith in 2025.

Of their 22 finals so far the Warriors have won nine and lost 13. Of the five they've played at Go Media Stadium they have won three.

The grand final will be played in Sydney on Sunday 4 October.

Week one: Qualifiers

The first week of playoffs will see the top four play qualifying finals.

1st v 4th ( Panthers vs Roosters) and

2nd v 3rd Warriors vs Dolphins)

This is where a top two finish is a huge benefit, as a win in week one means a week off and advancing straight to the preliminary finals in week three.

The bottom four will then play elimination finals:

5th v 8th (Sharks vs Cowboys) and

6th v 7th (Rabbitohs vs Knights)

These games are sudden death - lose and your season is over. Winners of these games will head to week two to meet the losers of the qualifiers.

The Warriors and Dolphins are one apiece in 2026, the Warriors winning 20-18 on Anzac Day in Wellington before the Dolphins claimed a 26-24 win in round 17.

The Warriors will get a second life in the NRL finals. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Week two: Semi-finals

The teams that lost their qualifying finals get another chance. They play the winners of the elimination finals in two semi-finals.

The two winners move on to the preliminary finals.

Likely match ups-

Roosters vs Sharks

Dolphins vs Rabbitohs

Week three- Preliminary final

The four remaining teams play in the preliminary finals.

The likely scenarios will see the Panthers and Warriors, should they win in week one, advance straight to the preliminaries to meet the winners of the semi finals.

Likely match ups-

Panthers vs Dolphins

Warriors vs Roosters

The winners book their place in the Grand Final.

Week four- Grand Final

The two preliminary-final winners meet in the NRL Grand Final.

All going to plan, the grand final will feature the top two teams.

ARLC Chairman Peter V'landys said the season has set records.

"Well over four million people attended matches and more than 150 million people watched our games."

World.title: Explainer: What are the rules around election advertising?
World.content:
Explainer - It's two months until Election Day and campaign billboards have been sprouting up like multicoloured weeds, with catchy slogans and smiling candidate portraits lining the roads.

Now that election season is starting to ramp up in earnest, what are the rules about campaign advertising?

There are many requirements around disclosure, campaign spending and the timing of certain election s.

Here's a rundown of what every hopeful candidate will need to know as they sprint to the finish line of Election Day on 7 November.

There are many rules in place for the election ads we'll see leading up to Election Day. RNZ illustration / Nik Dirga / 123rf

What counts as an ?

They can be in the humble newspaper, on television, leaflets dropped in your mailbox or ads seen while scrolling online, or they can be big old billboards you see every time you drive to the supermarket.

The Electoral Commission's candidate handbook defines them as "an  that may reasonably be regarded as encouraging or persuading voters to vote, or not vote, for a candidate or party", or alternatively, "a type of candidate or party the  describes by referencing views they do or don't hold".

What that all means is that it's anything that is trying to persuade you to vote a certain way.

Editorial content - news items such as RNZ reporting Christopher Luxon's latest announcement, for example - doesn't count as an .

Individuals posting their political views online doesn't count, unless it's paid content or someone claiming to speak for a political party, i.e. posting saying they speak for the Green Party or New Zealand First, for example.

An MP's contact details also do not count as election advertising, nor do columns or opinion pieces solicited or published by media with no payment involved.

There are no limitations on where candidates or advocacy groups can buy s, or how often they can buy them, other than the spending limits during that designated regulation period, the Advertising Standards Authority chief told RNZ earlier this year.

"The ASA does not restrict election s in those ways," its chief executive Hilary Souter said.

But if you are making an election ad, you've absolutely, positively got to include a promoter statement.

Campaign ads must carry a promoter statement, as seen at the bottom left on this National billboard. RNZ / Nik Dirga

What's a promoter statement, then?

Basically, it tells people who's behind the . Those small notes you see on billboards telling you "authorised by Joe Bloggs" or something similar? That's a promoter statement.

Promoter statements are required at all times, even outside the official regulatory period, and they must include a name and contact details.

Advocacy groups such as Council of Trade Unions or Family First NZ also fall in this requirement.

They need to be "clearly displayed," the Electoral Commission says - no 2-point font, please - and it notes "making your promoter statement too small will likely generate complaints".

If you don't use a promoter statement, you can be fined up to $40,000, so it's probably worth taking the time to credit your advert accordingly.

Elections NZ also can give advice on whether an ad counts as an election  or not, by contacting advisory@elections.govt.nz.

Election sign rules are set by local councils. RNZ / Nik Dirga

What about election billboards?

Election billboard rules are set by local councils and vary from place to place.

For example, in Auckland and Wellington, election signs are only allowed nine weeks before Election Day - which is why many places started seeing them go up this past weekend.

"You should talk to your local council before you put up any election signs," Elections NZ's website warns.

The Electoral Act says you can have election signs that are up to 3 square metres in size in the nine weeks before Election Day.

And all those billboards are required to have the mandatory promoter statement, preferably not at microscopic size.

But the internet is likely to be the biggest battlefield in Election 2026, not billboards.

Do all these rules apply in cyberspace?

The days of people only seeing election ads in newspapers and before the 6pm news are long past.

You're likely to soon be bombarded by election content every time you start scrolling on your phone.

Broadly, the rules are just the same for online s.

"Our election advertising rules are media-neutral in that the same requirements apply no matter where they appear," University of Otago professor of law Andrew Geddis said.

"As such, online election ads delivered through social media or elsewhere still must contain promoters statements that alert those receiving them as to who is behind the messages."

The election regulated period lays out spending rules. RNZ / Nik Dirga

What the election regulated period means

It's when we start counting how much is being spent, for one thing.

The regulated election period runs in the three months before Election Day - this year, it started 7 August and goes to 6 November.



Electorate candidates are only allowed to spend up to $36,000 during the regulated period. This includes any advertising by someone else that is approved by the candidate.

Registered political parties can spend up to $1,503,000 if they contest the party vote plus $36,000 for each electorate candidate for the party. Registered third party promoters can spend up to $424,000 while unregistered third party promoters can spend up to $17,000.

Electoral Commission's legal and policy manager Kristina Temel told RNZ earlier this year that there are also some requirements about how campaign advertising is conducted outside the regulatory period.

"The regulated period is relevant for election expenditure limits, but both before, during and after the regulated period, obligations regarding promoter statements and written authorisation to publish election s apply," she said.

And of course, all election advertising has to be taken down by midnight on 6 November, including billboards and online ads, and breaches can be fined.

The parties are now lobbying for your vote on 7 November. RNZ / Nik Dirga

Are media companies obligated to be fair in the ads they run?

There's no requirement for equal time, so if one party decides to buy more ads there's no obligation for media to run an equal amount by another. It's all about how much money political groups are willing to spend.

"Ultimately, the responsibility to be aware of and comply with all aspects of advertising regulation is shared between all the parties to an , including the advertiser, agencies, and media organisations," the Advertising Standards Code says.

And if ads are misleading or violate the rules, there are several ways to file a complaint about them.

So how do you make complaints?

The Electoral Commission deals with breaching of election advertising or Election Day rules under the Electoral Act, and election programmes under the Broadcasting Act. Offences could then be reported to the police.

When it comes to content, the Broadcasting Standards Authority, the Media Council and Advertising Standards Authority can all field possible complaints about election adverts that fall in their jurisdiction.

The BSA - which is set to be eliminated in the near future - oversees TV and radio, the ASA oversees ads in other media, and the Media Council looks at editorial content concerns.

"As in previous years, our focus will be on paid election advertising and compliance under the rules of social responsibility and truthful presentation," the ASA's Souter said.

World.title: Diesel spill north of Dunedin causes SH1 delays
World.content:
Motorists north of Dunedin have been facing disruption due to a diesel spill on State Highway 1.

Emergency services were alerted shortly before 6am on Monday.

Diesel had spilled onto both lanes of the highway.

State Highway 1 at Evansdale was closed at the Coast Road turnoffs between Evansdale and Hawksbury for several hours.

World.title: Fatal two-vehicle crash closes SH1 in Canterbury
World.content:
One person died and two others were seriously injured in a crash north of Ashburton on Monday morning.

The two-vehicle crash on Rakaia Highway north of Ashburton happened shortly after 5am.

On person died at the scene, and the two injured people were taken to hospital in a serious condition.

State Highway 1 was closed between Racecourse Road and Mitcham Road, with detours in place.

World.title: Auckland Airport plans change to security and passport control
World.content:
Passengers at Auckland Airport will see a change to the order of passport control and security screening from late 2027.

From then, international travellers will first go through security screening and then through passport control, Auckland Airport chief operations officer Chloe Surridge said.

The switch is part of a larger construction project to bring domestic jet and international operations under one roof.

"This change in sequencing will pave the way for how travellers are processed through the new terminal, within one building."

New Zealand Customs' Craig Chitty said the change to security screening first will create a safer environment for both travellers and staff.

"This sequencing is considered international best practice to help support a smoother customer experience. It creates a clearer separation between security screening and border control functions, and it supports greater safety for all.

"Customs is also about to embark on our eGate replacement programme at Auckland Airport, so aligning the upgrades of our eGates with 'the Flip' project will help minimise disruption throughout the transition."

World.title: Housing market continues to soften in three months to August - QV
World.content:
The housing market is continuing to weaken, according to Quotable Value's latest house price index.

In the three months to August, national house values slipped 1.9 percent, the largest quarterly fall in two years.

It comes after the index recorded residential property values falling by 1.5 percent nationally in the three months to the end of July.

QV said the average Kiwi home is now worth $894,977, down 1.7 percent since the start of the year and 1.3 percent less than the same time last year.

QV national spokesperson Simon Petersen said the latest figures showed buyers remained firmly in control as the market headed into spring.

He described the market as being in a slow deterioration rather than a sudden correction.

"Buyers have plenty of choice, they're taking their sweet time, they're negotiating hard, and they're prepared to walk away if the numbers don't stack up. That's putting downward pressure on property values."

The market softness was particularly evident in the major cities, according to the QV index.

Auckland's average home value fell by 2.7 percent in the quarter - its largest quarterly decline since August 2024, while Wellington recorded a 3.5 percent fall, its largest quarterly decline since March 2023.

Christchurch, which QV said had been one of the country's more resilient housing markets this year, slipped 0.5 percent - its first negative quarterly result in 11 months.

World.title: Coalition returned to government in new poll, as Opportunity loses kingmaker spot
World.content:
Labour and National are both polling below 30 percent in a new poll that also has Opportunity short of the threshold needed for getting into government.

The Quilae Wong-led upstarts have fallen from 6.1 to 4.5 percent in the latest Taxpayers' Union-Curia Poll, bucking the trend found in other polls.

Labour has taken a big hit, down 1.9 to 25.9 percent - its lowest result in this poll since July 2024, and even lower than the 26.9 point thrashing it got at the 2023 election.

National has also taken a tumble, down two points, to 29 percent - also significantly lower than the 38 percentage points it won at the last election.

The current coalition government would be returned to power based on this poll, with Opportunity unable to get above 5 percent and become kingmaker.

ACT and the Greens were the main beneficiaries of the major parties and Opportunity's collapse. The Greens were up 3.8 percentage points to 13.9 percent, and ACT up 3.2 to 10.5 percent.

New Zealand First was down 0.7 to 8.4 percent.

Te Pāti Māori gained 0.5 points to 2 percent. The party this year hopes to use MMP's overhang to boost the chance of removing the coalition.

Te Pāti Māori are trying to win all seven Māori seats, rather than boost their party vote. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Rounding out the party vote results were NZ Loyal (1.5 percent), Animal Justice (1.2), Women's Rights (0.7), Vision NZ (0.5) and the New Conservatives (0.5).

When it came to seats, the coalition - National, ACT and NZ First - would get 64 compared to the opposition - Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori - on 56. The right-leaning Taxpayers' Union's analysis assumes Te Pāti Māori would win three seats.

Opportunity would get zero on these results, being below the 5 percent threshold.

Christopher Luxon remained ahead of Chris Hipkins as preferred prime minister, down 2 percentage points to 21.2 percent. Hipkins fell 2.9 to 16.9 percent.

World.title: Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like in Brisbane boilover
World.content:
When Sydney chairman Andrew Pridham declared his side's premiership hopes "torpedoed" after suspending five players, he was right.

Preparing for a finals campaign is a delicate exercise. A little shift here or there can have major impacts. The less things change, the better.

At least, that is what conventional wisdom says.

Swans coach 'lost for words' after thumping Lions to book prelim berth Dean Cox reacts after seeing his undermanned side topple the two-time reigning premiers Brisbane at the SCG.

Last year, Adelaide's excellent home-and-away season was detonated by Izak Rankine's suspension for a homophobic slur on the eve of the finals.

Rankine's actions drew a dark cloud over the entire football club, and without him on the field in the finals, the Crows unsurprisingly limped out in straight sets.

Winning a final with five of your first-choice players sidelined? That seemed like mission impossible for the Swans.

A lot has been made of Sydney's famed "Bloods" culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. What is it? What is it supposed to look like? Is it real or just a PR myth?

While the club rightly admitted the culture was not what it once was off the field, on the field there appears to be little sign of slippage.

Sydney appeared to be the rank outsider heading into the finals after being decimated by club-imposed suspensions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

With Sydney decimated by the suspensions, the Swans appeared to be their rivals' easy ticket to a deep September run, the helpless carcass hungry animals in an African savanna would feast upon.

Brisbane, by virtue of a slight percentage edge over Hawthorn, had the apparent gift of facing the Swans in one qualifying final while the Hawks looked doomed as they headed to Perth to take on Fremantle in the other. How quickly things can change over one weekend.

Sydney has been one of the AFL's model clubs over the past two decades as a picture of professionalism from the top down, and performances like the one against Brisbane remind you exactly why the Swans have been revered for so long.

Turn on a Swans game, and you know what you're getting. Regardless of who is in the line-up or who is in the coaches' box, Sydney shows up with a baseline of effort and intensity, backed by a relentless never-say-die attitude.

The Swans paid tribute to the club's famed "Bloods" culture in its banner before the qualifying final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

All of these traits make up Sydney's true "Bloods" culture on the field.

If you wanted an example of what it looks like, the culture was on full display as Sydney eviscerated the two-time reigning premiers in front of an SCG crowd that was as raucous as it has ever been.

The louder the crowd got, the better the Swans played. The better the Swans played, the louder they got. The crowd and the players worked hand in hand like a beautiful symphony, and the tidal wave they created swallowed Brisbane up entirely.

It is hard to imagine an 18-5 team flying under the radar, but that is exactly what Sydney has done so far this season, right up until the Pullman Hotel scandal.

A serious knee injury to captain Callum Mills added an extra layer of adversity for the Swans against the Lions. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

While the AFL world was consumed by Fremantle's leap from a cute team to a bona fide premiership threat and Brisbane's bid to threepeat, Sydney quietly ticked along in the background to the best home-and-away season in its history.

What Sydney couldn't recoup in terms of talent in the absence of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — arguably three of its top six players by any metric — it made up for with sheer, unadulterated hard work against Brisbane.

That is not to say the Swans are a team bereft of star power in the absence of the suspended five.

In Charlie Curnow, Sydney still has the AFL's most terrifying key forward, in the metronomic Brodie Grundy, it still has arguably the best big man on his day in the non-Max Gawn division, in Errol Gulden, it has a Rolls-Royce of a midfielder capable of being the lead actor in any team's engine room, and in the incandescent Tom Papley, it has a small forward that can bend the energy of a match like no other.

Charlie Curnow continued his excellent debut season with the Swans with another bag of goals against the Lions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It is no surprise that all of these guys, as well as many others, were excellent in the win over Brisbane.

"The two weeks of training up to that point, we trained the house down," Papley told Nine's Sunday Footy Show about the lead-up to the Lions game.

"That's the best we've trained all season. The drills we did were all about pressure, closing space, chasing, tackling, and surging the ball forward, and we trained so well and came together on game day.

"I'm so proud of the boys. It was amazing.

"There were board members in the rooms after the game saying it was the best win in the club's history apart from the premierships.

"The job's not done yet, but the desire and passion we played with … inside the four walls we believed and that's what we kept doing."

Sydney has played in, and won, bigger games in its history. It will continue to do so going forward as well.

But with the context of everything that has happened in the lead-up to this one, and then the Callum Mills injury sprinkled over the top as an additional bit of nightmare fuel, Sydney will have to go a long way to find a performance it is prouder of.

The Swans still face an uphill task to win this year's flag, even with a home preliminary final to come in a fortnight.

As the Swans have experienced in their past four Grand Final appearances since their last premiership in 2012, even the best-laid plans with a perfect lead-up can go up in smoke on the final day of the season.

But for one day at least, the Swans showed everyone just exactly what "Bloods" culture is supposed to look like.

World.title: 'Owe my life to you': Driver stops to pull rival out of flaming Ferrari
World.content:
A young Dutch racer is being hailed as a "superhero" after stopping on a race track to help pull a fellow competitor out of his flaming car.

The incident happened on Saturday in the China GT series in Shanghai, when 36-year-old British driver Ollie Millroy was part of a multi-car crash in his Ferrari.

The car was then engulfed in flames, and the situation grew more desperate because there were no safety marshals in the area.

Dutch competitor Loek Hartog, 23, stopped, ran over to the flaming car and tried to help Millroy out of the driver's side door.

Unable to free Millroy, Hartog then grabbed a nearby fire extinguisher and doused the flames enough so he could then pull his rival out of the other side of the car.

"I owe my life to you," Millroy wrote on social media.

"Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight, and risked his own life to get me out of the car. I don't remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and 1 hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life.

"One day I will tell our three kids this story, and Loek will be the biggest superhero in history in their eyes too."

Millroy said he broke five ribs, as well as his collarbone, hand, and finger and sustained a bruised lung from the wreck.

Hartog wrote on social media that Millroy had nothing to thank him for, saying he wished anyone else in his position had done the same.

"I wish to live in a world where this would not be considered as bravery but as instinct of others too," Hartog wrote.

"I am so thankful to have been right at the place I needed to be in space and time."

Chinese-owned news website Global Times reported that organisers of the China GT Championship would review "shortcomings" in the series' safety protocols, among other areas for improvement.

"After the race, we will further review and investigate the accident and formulate more comprehensive plans to address shortcomings in competition organisation, support, emergency response, rescue and medical services," organisers said in a statement.

World.title: F1 wonderkid wins from 19th, Piastri fifth as Ferrari fans left in tears
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli's magical season has continued emphatically, winning his home Italian Grand Prix from 19th in a historic triumph for the F1 drivers' championship leader.

The 20-year-old drove a near-flawless race to become the first Italian in 60 years to win in their home grand prix, beating teammate George Russell in a thrilling finish.

Max Verstappen placed third, while Lando Norris overtook Oscar Piastri on the final lap as the McLaren duo finished fourth and fifth.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc suffered a heavy crash into the barriers on the second lap, hitting the tyre wall at high speed and shattering the hearts of thousands of passionate Ferrari fans in the grandstands at Monza.

But those Ferrari fans were on their feet by the end of the grand prix, as one of their own took the chequered flag on a weekend where his championship lead was supposed to shrink.

"Unbelievable. I am so happy," Antonelli said after becoming the first Italian since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966 to win the race.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Italian GP 1. 267 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes 2. 201 — George Russell, Mercedes 3. 191 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari 4. 171 — Lando Norris, McLaren 5. 155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari 6. 127 — Max Verstappen, Red Bull 7. 116 — Oscar Piastri, McLaren

"I could never have imagined to be here today.

"We managed to pull it off, and I am really happy."

Antonelli's win from 19th is the second-furthest back a driver has started and gone on to win.

Only John Watson, from 22nd at the 1983 United States Grand Prix, has won from a lower grid spot.

Antonelli knew he was going to start from well back, with Mercedes announcing at the Dutch Grand Prix a fortnight earlier that the championship leader would have new power unit components fitted for this weekend, which would exceed his year's allocation.

With tyre degradation low, and a one-stop all but certain if there were no incidents, Antonelli got off to a flying start by jumping from 19th to 12th in the opening two laps.

Leclerc lost control of his Ferrari at the final turn of the second lap, ploughing into the barriers, knocking him out of the grand prix and bringing out a red flag.

A marshal consoles Charles Leclerc after crashing out of the Italian Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Alex Bierens de Haan)

Leclerc's crash was too much for some Ferrari fans to bear, seen on the television broadcast crying and needing to be consoled.

Ferrari fan crying, consoled, after Charles Leclerc crashed out of the Italian Grand Prix. (Kayo/Fox Sports)

All drivers were able to make their mandatory tyre change, which led to leader Russell, who took that position from surprise Alpine pole sitter Pierre Gasly on lap two, with hard compound tyres to get to the end of the race.

Antonelli, who started on hards, had to use the slightly quicker but less durable mediums for the rest of the race.

Russell held the lead off the restart, Verstappen moved into second as Gasly fell down the order, and Antonelli continued to pick his way through the field.

By lap 16, Antonelli passed Verstappen and then he had the lead two laps later.

Antonelli and Russell would trade the lead over the next few laps, as Monza's powerful slipstream and the use of electrical power boosts, lead to drivers swapping positions in what has come to be called yo-yo racing.

Mercedes told their drivers to stop squabbling in a bid to distance themselves from Verstappen, who was just holding onto them.

Aston Martin's Lance Stroll stopped just off the track on lap 28, resulting in a virtual safety car being called — and the decisive moment in the race.

Mercedes kept race leader Russell out on his hards, but brought Antonelli in for new mediums.

When racing resumed, Antonelli was sixth and 15 seconds behind Russell with 24 laps to go.

With fresher tyres, Antonelli stormed back to the rear of his teammate, setting up an epic finish.

The 20-year-old went onto the gravel on lap 49 in an unsuccessful attempt to take the lead.

On the next lap, Antonelli made no mistake and made the race-winning move to the delight of the Italian crowd.

"It was quite scary in the moment [going into the gravel]," Antonelli said of his gravel trip on lap 49.

"I was like, 'maybe I lost my chance'.

"Luckily we still had the pace and managed to bring it home."

Antonelli's lead over Russell in the drivers' championship now extends to 66 points.

The mountain for Russell to win a maiden world championship this year just got steeper, and he is left with the disappointment of having his deficit extended despite starting 17 grid places ahead of Antonelli.

Asked about Mercedes's decision to leave him on track during the virtual safety car, Russell said he did not think Antonelli would be called into the pits.

"I thought we were both going to stay out, I was surprised to see him pitting," Russell said.

"In the end, it was a roll of the dice both ways.

"In the moment, the team wouldn't have known which strategy was better. It made sense to split the cars, but in the end, Kimi had great pace."

Verstappen finished third, after a terrific late battle with Piastri for the final podium spot.

The Australian, however, was unable to hold onto fourth, losing that place to his teammate Norris on the final lap of the grand prix.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was sixth, pole sitter Gasly was seventh, and Racing Bulls youngster Arvid Lindblad placed eighth.

Franco Colapinto recovered from an early excursion into a gravel trap to place ninth for Alpine.

Japan's Yuki Tsunoda, driving for Racing Bulls while Liam Lawson fills in for the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, claimed 10th and one championship point.
